GUIDE

🎯 How to Use This Full Pack

• Work through the sections in exam order (Income Tax → CGT → IHT → CT → VAT) or jump straight to a topic via the ☰ sidebar.

• Answer each question — select an option (or type a number, or click the ✓ cells for tick-box tables). You get instant green/red feedback and the worked solution auto-reveals.

• Multi-answer questions ("Which TWO...") use checkboxes — select all correct options.

• Examiner's reports & tutor tips appear inside each solution — these are exactly what ACCA markers look for.

• Use ⚡ Quick Fire for a 20-question random warm-up, or ⏱ Mock 25 for a timed 25-question Section A simulation.

• Progress is saved automatically in your browser (localStorage). Use 🖨 to print or save as PDF.

For the first two tax years after leaving the UK, what is the maximum number of ties which

✅ Answer: C

provided to you in the examination.
This question could have been answered quickly and easily provided that you understood how

Q4 · Question 4
+10 XPA · MCQ
4 March 2019 OT question
Hana was UK resident in the tax year 2024/25. He worked full time in Egypt in the tax year
2025/26.
What is the maximum number of days which Hana can spend in the UK and be treated as
automatically not resident in the UK for the tax year 2025/26?
✅ Answer: C
📋 Examiner’s Report

This question examines the third automatic non-UK residency test. For an individual to meet
this test, and therefore be treated as automatically not resident in the UK for the tax year
2025/26, they would have to work full-time overseas and spend less than 91 days in the UK.
Therefore, because Hana worked full-time in Egypt throughout 2025/26, he will be treated
as automatically not resident in the UK for the tax year as long as he spends no more than 90
days in the UK.
The correct answer is therefore C, however, answer option A was most commonly chosen.
This would be the correct answer using the sufficient ties tests. However, the sufficient ties
tests are only used to determine residence status if none of the automatic non-UK residence
tests (and none of the automatic UK residence tests) is met.
This suggests that candidates may not have be en familiar enough with the residence tests
and the procedure to determine residence.

Q5 · Question 5
+10 XPA · MCQ
5 September/December 2021 OT question
Ella arrived in the UK to work as a nanny on 1 February 2025. She has never previously visited
the UK.
Ella lived with a family, for whom she did substantive, but not full-time work, until 31 August
2025.
On 1 September 2025 Ella left the UK to attend university in another country.
As a result of this visit to the UK, Ella stayed in the UK for 65 days during the tax year 2024/25
and 148 days during the tax year 2025/26. For these two tax years, Ella was neither
automatically not resident in the UK nor automatically resident.
What is Ella's UK residency status for each of the tax years 2024/25 and 2025/26?
✅ Answer: D
5 D
As Ella has not previously been resident in the UK then she will need to have four UK ties to
be UK resident in 2024/25 and will need two UK ties to be UK resident in 2025/26.
Ella has two UK ties, substantive work in the UK and available accommodation in the UK
(she lives with the family) and is therefore UK resident in 2025/26 but not 2024/25.

Q8 · Question 8
+10 XPA · MCQ
8 March 2020 OT question
Dane and Zara are a married couple.
They jointly own a residential property which is let to tenants. In the tax year 2025/26 the
property business income from the property is £20,000. Dane owns 25% of the property and
Zara owns the other 75%. No election has been made in relation to the ownership of the
property.
Zara earns employment income of £85,000 and Dane receives £2,252 of child benefit in the
tax year 2025/26. Dane has no other income.
Which TWO of the following statements are true in relation to Zara’s income tax liability
for the tax year 2025/26?
allowance (the “marriage allowance”)
Revenue & Customs (HMRC) specifying their actual ownership share in the residential
property
⚡ Select ALL correct options (A, D)
✅ Answer: A, D
8 A, D
Zara’s taxable income is £82,430, which is calculated as follows:
£
Employment income 85,000
Property business income (£20,000 × 50%) 10,000
––––––
95,000
Personal allowance (12,570)
––––––
Taxable income 82,430
––––––
Zara’s adjusted net income is above £80,000, therefore a child benefit income tax charge will
arise equal to the full amount of child benefit received by Dane, i.e. £2,252.
💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

Income generated from assets which are owned jointly is split 50:50 between spouses
regardless of the actual ownership percentage, unless an election is made to use the actual
ownership percentage.
The child benefit tax charge is taxed on the spouse or civil partner with income exceeding
£60,000, who is not necessarily the spouse in receipt of the benefit.

📋 Examiner’s Report

Statement B is incorrect. It is not possible for Zara to claim the transferable personal
allowance from Dane, as she is a higher rate taxpayer. In order to claim the transferable
personal allowance neither spouse/civil partner can be a higher or additional rate taxpayer.
Statement C is also incorrect. It would not be beneficial to Zara to make a joint election to
HMRC specifying their actual ownership share in the property. In doing so, Zara would be
taxed on 75% of the property income, i.e. £15,000 (20,000 × 75%). This would increase Zara’s
tax liability for the tax year 2025/26 and it would also mean that more of the income would
be taxed at the higher rate of 40%, than under the current 50:50 split.

Q17 · Question 17
+10 XPA · MCQ
17 Manon purchased £200,000 (nominal value) gilts, paying interest at 1%, for £211,000 on
1 September 2024. Interest is payable half yearly on 30 June and 31 December.
He sold the gilts on 1 December 2025 for £213,000 (including accrued interest).
How much will Manon include in savings income in respect of the gilts in the tax year
2025/26?
✅ Answer: D
17 D
£
Interest received 30 June 2025 (£200,000 × 1% × 6/12) 1,000
Interest accrued (1 July 2025 – 30 November 2025)
(£200,000 × 1% × 5/12)

833
––––––
Total interest income 1,833
––––––
💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

Gilt interest is taxed like other interest income on the receipts basis. However, under the
accrued income scheme when gilts are sold, interest is effectively allocated to the vendor and
purchaser on the accruals basis up to the date of sale.
Manon did not receive any interest on 31 December 2025 but will be taxed on £833
representing the interest accruing in the interest period for which he owned the gilts.

Q21 · Question 21
+10 XPA · MCQ
21 September/December 2020 OT question
On 1 October 2025, Sou granted a 25-year lease of a freehold property in return for a premium
of £20,000.
What is Sou’s taxable property income for the tax year 2025/26 in respect of this lease
premium?
✅ Answer: A
21 A
£
Premium 20,000
Less: £20,000 × 2% × (25
– 1) (9,600)
–––––––
Property income 10,400
–––––––
Alternative calculation = £20,000 × (51 – 25)/50 = £10,400
📋 Examiner’s Report

The premium received is on a short lease therefore a proportion of it is treated as income.
£10,400 being the correct income portion of the premium.
(B) Calculates the capital portion of the premium £20,000 × 2% × (25 ─ 1) = £9,600
(C) Calculates the correct part of the premium but it is unnecessarily time apportioned (since
Sou is the lessor and is taxed to income on receipt of the premium) £10,400 × 6/12 = £5,200
(D) £20,000 less (2% × (25) × £20,000) = £10,000 This does not deduct one year from 'n', the
number of years on the lease.

£

34 £600

Annual events which cost the employer more than £150 per head are a taxable benefit for the

📋 Examiner’s Report

This question required students to demonstrate their knowledge of capital allowances on cars,
where there was a disposal of a car during the year which was also used for private use by Olive.
As the car was disposed of during the year, ca ndidates need to recognise that a balancing
allowance arose on its disposal, and that the amount of capital allowance Olive could claim
was restricted to the business use element (i.e. 60%). The correct answer was therefore A.
Many candidates instead chose D, continuing to write down the cost of the car, rather than
calculating a balancing allowance. Candidates ar e reminded that cars which are used partly
for private use by a sole trader are put into their own pool and on disposal a balancing charge
or allowance may arise.

Q39 · Question 39
+10 XPA · MCQ
39 Which TWO of the following assets bought by a sole trader using the accruals basis will be
allocated to the main pool for capital allowance purposes?
2 emissions of 45 grams per kilometre costing £17,500 with 25% private
use by an employee of the business
business purposes by the owner of the business
⚡ Select ALL correct options (C, F)
✅ Answer: C and F
39 C and F
Any asset with private use by the owner of the business is allocated to a private use asset
column rather than the main pool.
Cars with CO₂ emissions in excess of 50 grams per kilometre are allocated to the special rate
pool rather than the main pool.
Long life assets (those with an expected life of 25 years or more, with a total cost of £100,000
in a twelve-month period) are added to the special rate pool. Assets with an expected
working life of less than 25 years are not treated as long life assets and are added to the main
pool.

order. It does not have to be offset against the prior year trading profit, or the savings income
in the current or prior year before this loss carry back.

Q51 · Question 51
+10 XPA · MCQ
51 Sally has been trading as a sole trader for many years. In the year ended 31 March 2026 she
made a trading loss of £45,000.
Sally’s only other source of income is property income of £8,000 each tax year.
In the tax year 2025/26 Sally realised a chargeable gain of £32,000 on the sale of a necklace
and a capital loss of £4,000 on the sale of a painting. She has capital losses brought forward
of £18,000.
What is the amount of trading loss that Sally can offset against her chargeable gain in the
tax year 2025/26?
✅ Answer: D
51 D
£
Available loss is lower of:
(i) Remaining trading loss following current year claim against
total income (£45,000 – £8,000) 37,000
––––––
(ii) CY chargeable gains 32,000
Less: CY capital losses (4,000)
Less: Capital losses b/f (18,000)
––––––
10,000
––––––
Available loss 10,000
––––––
💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

The maximum amount of trading loss that can be offset against chargeable gains is the lower
of:
(i) the remaining loss, or
(ii) chargeable gains in the year after the deduction of current year capital losses and
brought forward capital losses. Brought forward capital losses are not restricted to
preserve the annual exempt amount in this calculation.
The maximum trading loss is then offset against current year chargeable gains, after current
year capital losses but before brought forward capital losses. The offset of brought forward
capital losses is deducted before the annual exempt amount, therefore the annual exempt
amount will be preserved.

Q53 · Question 53
+10 XPA · MCQ
53 December 2018 OT question
Humphrey is a sole trader who has been trading for a number of years.
Humphrey incurred a trading loss in the tax year 2025/26. He wishes to make a claim to offset
this loss against his total income of the tax year 2024/25.
What is the deadline for Humphrey to claim this relief?
PENSIONS AND NIC
✅ Answer: B
📋 Examiner’s Report

This question examines knowledge of the deadlin e for an individual taxpayer to claim relief
for a trading loss which they wish to offset in the tax year prior to the tax year in which the
loss arose. The correct answer is option B (31 January 2028), as a claim must be made within
one year of 31 January following the end of the tax year in which the loss arose. Therefore,
as the loss arose in the tax year 2025/26, a claim for relief must be made by 31 January 2028.
Option B was the most common answer selected but a significant number of candidates also
chose each of the other answer options, suggesting that many candidates were not well
prepared for a question on this topic. The second most common answer was option A
(31 January 2027) which is the deadline for submitting a personal tax return online for the
tax year 2025/26. Candidates may have selected this date as they are familiar with this
deadline in relation to the tax year 2025/26 and assumed the deadline for claiming the loss
would be the same.
Administration deadlines, both for individuals and companies, are an important part of the
syllabus and future candidates are reminded of the importance of learning, and being able
to distinguish between, the different deadlines as part of their studies.
PENSIONS AND NIC

Employer pension contributions are an exempt benefit.
Tax relief for occupational pension scheme contributions is given at the employee’s marginal

Q65 · Question 65

65 Isaac is self-employed and for the year ended 31 March 2026 he paid £20,000 (net) into his
personal pension plan. Isaac’s relevant earnings for the tax year 2025/26 were £110,000.
What amount of income tax will Isaac pay at the basic rate for the tax year 2025/26?

£

£
✅ Answer: £12,540
65 £12,540
Isaac’s income tax basic rate band is extended by the grossed up contribution as follows:
£37,700 + (£20,000 × 100/80) = £62,700
Income tax of £12,540 (£62,700 × 20%) is payable at the basic rate.
The contribution is lower than Isaac’s relevant earnings for the year (£110,000) and therefore
tax relief is available on the full amount.

Austin’s total gross pension contributions are £28,000 (£22,400 × 100/80). They are less than
his relevant earnings of £51,200 and less than the annual allowance. His contributions are
fully tax relievable.
Petra’s gross contributions of £82,500 (£66,000 × 100/80) exceed the annual allowance of
£60,000 for the tax year 2025/26. She has no unused annual allowances brought forward as
she was not a member of a pension scheme in previous years. She will obtain tax relief at
source on the contributions, as they are less than her relevant earnings. However, part of the
tax relief will be clawed back through an annual allowance charge.
💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

An employed individual can make pension contributions into either an occupational pension
scheme or a personal pension scheme or both. Contributions are fully tax relievable provided
total gross contributions do not exceed their total relevant earnings and the annual
allowance.

+10 XPA · MCQ
69 December 2019 OT question
Niamhe has adjusted income for the tax year 2025/26 of £330,000.
During the year, she made personal pension scheme contributions of £100,000 (gross).

for the tax year 2025/26?
ADMINISTRATION AND ETHICS
✅ Answer: A
69 A
£ £
Adjusted income 330,000
–––––––

Annual allowance – 2025/26 60,000
Less: 50% × (£330,000 – £260,000) (35,000)
––––––
Available annual allowance 25,000

📋 Examiner’s Report

This is a fairly challenging question involvin g a number of rules and computational steps.
Candidates should first calculate the annual allowance, followed by the annual allowance
charge.
The correct answer is A because, the annual allowance of £60,000 is reduced by £1 for every
£2 by which the individual’s adjusted income exceeds the threshold of £260,000, subject to
a minimum annual allowance of £10,000. So, Niamhe’s annual allowance for the tax year
2025/26 is £25,000. The annual allowance charge is the amount by which Niamhe’s gross
personal pension scheme contributions exceed her annual allowance.
A number of candidates selected D £25,000, which is the annual allowance, rather than the
annual allowance charge.

84 £17,000

The payments on account are payable in two equal instalments on 31 January in the tax year

payment would be due on 31 January after the end of the tax year (31 January 2027).

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

For the tax year 2025/26 this is 31 January 2027.
Where the balancing payment is made:
• more than one month late, penalty = 5%
• more than six months late = an additional 5% is charged (total of 10%)
• more than 12 months late = a further 5% is charged (total of 15%).

Q88 · Question 88
+10 XPA · MCQ
88 June 2023 OT question
Ruby was required to make payments on account of £5,000 in total towards her tax liability
for the tax year 2025/26.

that her tax liability for that year is £7,000.
Ruby pays her balancing payment of £2,000 on 31 January 2027.
How much late payment interest will Ruby have to pay in relation to her tax liability for the
tax year 2025/26?
✅ Answer: A
88 A
The correct answer is £89 (£2,500 × 8.5% × 5/12).
Ruby’s payments on account are due on 31 January 2026 and 31 July 2026 with the balancing
payment due on 31 January 2027. Therefore, her first payment on account was late by five
months (from 31 January 2026 to 30 June 2026, the day before she paid the tax). The rate of
interest on underpaid tax is given to you in the Tax Tables in the exam and is shown there as
8.5%.

🔑 Key Answer Tips

This case OT involves the income tax position for two individuals with different
circumstances. It tests income tax, knowledge of NIC and pension contributions. All the topics
are covered at a basic level and should therefore have been manageable.

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

Savings income falling in the first £5,000 of taxable income is taxed at the starting rate of 0%.
In addition, basic rate taxpayers are entitled to a nil rate band of £1,000 for savings income.
The starting rate band and the savings nil rate band use the basic rate and higher rate bands.



The total available annual allowance is the allowance for the current tax year plus unused
allowances from the previous three tax years, provided the individual was a member of a
pension scheme in the tax year.

Always check carefully whether you have been given payments gross or net.
5
True False
His basic rate band for the tax year 2025/26 would have been
increased by £8,600 in relation to this contribution ✓
His taxable income for the tax year 2025/26 would have been
reduced by £8,600 ✓
HM Revenue & Customs would have paid £1,376 into the
pension fund on his behalf ✓
His personal allowance would have increased by £4,300 in the
tax year 2025/26 ✓

Statement 2 is incorrect because personal pension contributions do not affect taxable income.
Instead basic rate tax relief is given at source and higher rate relief is given by extending the
basic and higher rate bands by the amount of the gross contribution of £8,600 (£6,880 ×
100/80).
Statement 3 is incorrect because HM Revenue & Customs would have contributed £1,720 i.e.
the basic rate tax deducted at source (£6,880 × 20/80).
Statement 1 is correct because the basic rate band for 2025/26 is extended by the gross
amount of the personal pension contributions (£6,880 × 100/80= £8,600). This reduces the
income falling in the higher rate band by £8,600.
Statement 4 is correct as Charles’ adjusted net income would have been £8,600 lower as a
result of deducting the gross personal pension contribution of £8,600. This would increase the
personal allowance by £8,600 × 50% = £4,300 as the ANI in excess of £100,000 has decreased.

Benefits are a highly examinable area and the detailed rules must be learnt.

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

Loss relief claimed against total income is capped at the higher of £50,000 and 25% of
adjusted total income (25% × £361,990 = £90,498). Therefore there is full relief for the
£58,000 loss against total income.

🔑 Key Answer Tips

This case OT involves the employment income ru les, especially benefits. It also covers the
adjustment of the personal allowance and a question on NIC computations. The last question
is relatively straightforward provided the key facts about national insurance contributions
had been learnt.

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

Travel between home and office is ordinary commuting which does not qualify for tax relief.

The question states that the average method is used to calculate the taxable benefit, so do
not waste time also preparing calculations using the precise (or accurate) method which will
score no marks.

––––––

Long service awards are exempt where there has been at least 20 years of service by the
employee and where the cost is £50 or less for each year of service.

The employment allowance of £10,500 is available per employer, not per employee.
The taxable mileage allowance paid in respect of home to office travel is cash earnings and is
subject to class 1 NIC.
Non-cash benefits are not subject to class 1 NICs – they are subject to class 1A.
Class 1 primary NICs are payable at 8% on earnings above £12,570, but this drops to 2% on
earnings above £50,270.

📋 Examiner’s Report

The income tax question involved Jason. He was employed by Initial plc as a sales manager,
but was considering resigning on 14 March 2025 and taking up an offer of employment with
Subsequent plc which would commence on 15 March 2025. If employed by Subsequent plc,
Jason would receive a higher base salary and more benefits compared to remaining
employed by Initial plc. However, Jason wanted to know how much more income tax he
would have to pay should he take up the new offer of employment.
Part (a) for 2 marks required candidates to state one advantage and one disadvantage for an
employee if their employer payrolled the taxabl e benefits provided to the employee. This
section was not particularly well answered.
Rather than just being asked to explain payro lling of benefits, candidates are also expected
to know the advantages and disadvantages if an employer payrolls the taxable benefits
provided to an employee. For example, an advantage to the employee could be either:
• There is no need to declare payrolled benefits on the employee’s self-assessment tax
return, or
• The employee will not have any unexpected tax liabilities in respect of the taxable
benefits which have been payrolled.
And a disadvantage would be:
• The tax due on the benefit will generally be paid earlier than if collected under self-
assessment.
Part (b) for 11 marks required a calculation of how much more income tax Jason would have
had to pay for the tax year 2025/26 if he took up the offer of employment with Subsequent
plc rather than remaining employed by Initial plc. This section was reasonably well answered.
• Candidates should simply list any exempt items within the main computation and
indicate as such by the use of zero (0) – not by an explanation.
• Even though there might only be a ½ mark fo r recognising an exemption, it is important
to know the various exemptions so that time is not spent in producing more
complicated workings.
• Candidates should note that many of the workings for this style of question can be
included within the main computation. For example, the beneficial loan working
(£140,000 × 3.75% × 8/12 = £3,500). The only aspect which warranted a separate
working here was the living accommodation additional benefit.
• With computations containing both additions and deductions, candidates should be
very careful to indicate which is which. A single column approach with deductions
included as such on the spreadsheet avoids any confusion.
• Jason was clearly an additional rate taxpayer under both employment alternatives, so
the extra amount of income tax payable was simply the difference between the two
amounts of employment income multiplied by the rate of 45%. Producing two income
tax workings not only used more time, but meant that a mistake was much more likely.
Practice as many computations as possible. If this is done, straightforward workings for the
main benefits should become second nature, meaning that marks can be obtained quite
quickly without making any basic mistakes.

Part (c) for 2 marks required candidates (if Jason decided to resign as an employee of
Initial plc) to explain the main content and purpose of PAYE form P45. This section was not
particularly well answered.
If a requirement is just for two marks, then just a few brief points are required in an answer.
Of course, it is also important to know the difference between the different PAYE forms. The
following answer would have been sufficient:
• Form P45 will have shown Jason’s taxable earnings and income tax deducted up to the
date of leaving, together with the tax code at this date.
• Jason will have given a copy of the form to Subsequent plc so that they can correctly
calculate PAYE for the remainder of 2024/25.

The three requirements were all fairly straightforward, so it was surprising that this question
was not better answered.
Requirement (a) – 10 marks
Although the employment aspects of this requirement were well answered by most
candidates, a number of candidates struggled to correctly allocate the trading loss. The
interaction of capital allowances and loss relief was a particular issue. The calculation of the
accrued gilt income also caused problems.
• The car benefit should have represented two easy marks, but some candidates omitted
the 4% diesel surcharge, and the restriction by 8/12ths (the car only being provided
for eight months) was also sometimes incorrectly calculated or omitted altogether.
• Most candidates recognised that only on e of the mobile telephones was chargeable,
but the 20% basis of tax charge was less well known.
With regard to the trading loss, very few candidates appreciated that the balancing allowance
from the disposal of the car had to be added to the trading loss before allocating the resultant
loss.
The balancing allowance was simply:
• The brought forward written down value of £8,400
• Less the sale proceeds of £5,400
• Restricted to the business use proportion of 30%.
Many candidates overcomplicated this working by claiming allowances prior to the disposal,
with others not even realising there was a balancing event.
Having calculated a revised trading loss, the profit allocated should have been quite
straightforward. However, candidates often wasted time by not restricting their calculation
to just Poppy’s share of the £20,400 loss. The shares for Rose and Teasel were not relevant
and their calculation did not score any marks.
With Poppy receiving one-third of profits and losses for three months, and 50% thereafter,
the calculation for 2 marks was simply:
(£20,400 × 3/12 × 1/3) + (£20,400 × 9/12 × 1/2) = £9,350
When it comes to calculating accrued interest, candidates should remember that the relevant
figures are the nominal value and the interest rate. The gilts had a nominal value of £40,000,
an interest rate of 3%, and were owned for three months. The accrued interest calculation
for 1.5 marks was therefore:
£40,000 at 3% × 3/12 = £300
Requirement (b) – 2 marks
This requirement was answered quite poorly.
• For the first mark, candidates simply had to say that the related income tax liability is
collected under PAYE (or through payroll).
• For the second mark, it was necessary to state there is no reporting on form P11D.
Although some candidates picked up the first mark, very many candidates then went on to
say that reporting on form P11D (or some other form) was required.
Requirement (c) – 3 marks
This requirement was generally well answered by most candidates. The key point was
appreciating that the due date for the bala ncing payment was 31 January 2026, so the
payment was made seven months late.
The interest charge was therefore £2,600 × 8.5% × 7/12 = £129 for 1.5 marks.
A few candidates used the official rate of interest rather than the rate for underpaid tax.
As regards penalties, there were two 5% charges; the first for being one month late and the
second for being six months late.
Candidates should realise that where a requireme nt is just for three marks, then no more
than two or three short calculations or sentences are required. Also, answers should be
related to the information provided, so a long, detailed, explanation of the interest and
penalty rules in general is not going to score well.
🔑 Key Answer Tips

This section C question covers employment income, the accrued income scheme,
partnerships and administration.
Part (a) offers some easy marks for calculating basic employment benefits, but also has some
trickier marks on the accrued income scheme. Do your best here and move on!
Part (b) focuses on the administration of tax for employees. Administration can represent
quick and easy marks in the exam if you have learnt the rules. So make sure you know them.
Finally, part (c) looks at intere st and penalties in respect of late payment of a balancing
charge. Elements of the self-assessment system are often tested, so make sure you know the
implications if deadlines are not met, as well as what the deadlines are.

+10 XPC · CONSTRUCTED
KAZUO
This scenario relates to five requirements.
You should assume that today’s date is 25 March 2025 and the tax rates and allowances
for the tax year 2025/26 apply throughout.
Kazuo is currently employed at a gross annual salary of £200,000. Kazuo will continue to earn
the same salary until he retires on 5 April 2029, at which point his income will reduce to gross
annual pension income of £55,000. This means that Kazuo is currently an additional rate
taxpayer, but will only be a higher rate taxpayer from when he retires on 5 April 2029.
Kazuo will undertake £40,000 of work on a freelance basis during the year ended 5 April 2026.
To carry out this work, Kazuo will form a new limited company, Zaoku Ltd, of which he will
be an employee. This freelance work will not involve any expenditure and will last for just
one year, from 6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026. Zaoku Ltd will prepare accounts for the year
ended 5 April 2026.

Kazuo is looking at three alternative ways of extracting the profits of Zaoku Ltd:
Alternative 1
After allowing for corporation tax, Kazuo will withdraw the entire net of tax profits as
dividends during the tax year 2025/26.
Alternative 2
Zaoku Ltd will pay Kazuo gross directors' remuneration of £8,000 and Zaoku Ltd will make a
pension contribution of £32,000 into a company occupational pension scheme on Kazuo's
behalf during the tax year 2025/26. Kazuo ha s sufficient unused pension annual allowances
so that a pension contribution of this amount will not result in an annual allowance charge.
Alternative 3
Kazuo will not withdraw any amounts during the tax year 2025/26. Instead, the net of tax
profits will be left undrawn in Zaoku Ltd until the tax year 2029/30 when Kazuo has retired.
He will then withdraw the entire net of tax amount as dividends in the tax year 2029/30.
Kazuo does not have any other income.

5 April 2026, and will do this via a new limited company, Zaoku Ltd.
Kazuo was looking at three alternative ways of extracting the profits of Zaoku Ltd:
Alternative 1: After allowing for corporation tax, Kazuo will withdraw the entire net of tax
profits as dividends during the tax year 2025/26.
Alternative 2: Kazuo will be paid gross directors' remuneration of £8,000 and Zaoku Ltd will
make a pension contribution of £32,000 into a company occupational pension scheme on
Kazuo's behalf during the tax year 2025/26.
Alternative 3: The net of tax profits will be left undrawn in Zaoku Ltd until the tax year
2029/30 when Kazuo has retired. He will then withdraw the entire net of tax amount as
dividends in the tax year 2029/30.
Although there were a number of perfect answers, many candidates found this question
quite challenging. One particular problem was that candidates did not appreciate that part
(c) was essentially the same as part (a), but set a few years ahead with a lower tax rate. This
future setting confused a significant minority of candidates, with a number calculating
income and taxes over several years. However, the question clearly stated that the freelance
work would only last for just one year, from 6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026.
Requirement (a) – 3 marks
This requirement was generally fairly well answered, and there were many perfect answers.
Although candidates had the option of using a full calculation approach, working at the
margin was easier and quicker. There was also less scope for making arithmetical errors.
Unless opting for a full computation approach, the only relevance of Kazuo’s salary of
£200,000 was to establish the rate of tax applicable (and it was stated that Kazuo was an
additional rate taxpayer in any case). However, a number of candidates included this amount
within their corporation tax computation, and this then had a knock-on effect throughout
the remainder of the answer.
If using a working at the margin approach for the income tax calculation, this was simply (for
two marks):
£40,000 (freelance earnings) – £7,600 (corporation tax as calculated) – £500 (dividend nil rate
band) multiplied by the dividend additional tax rate of 39.35%
Common problems included using the gross earnings (rather than the net of tax figure) and
using an incorrect rate of tax. Given the rates of tax are provided, it made no sense to lose a
half-mark by carelessly using, for example, 39.55% instead of 39.35%.
Requirement (b) – 4 marks
This requirement caused the most problems, although it was more straightforward than
many candidates appreciated.
Corporation tax: Paying the director’s remuneration and making the pension contribution
simply reduced Zaoku Ltd’s taxable total profits (and corporation tax liability) to £0 (£40,000
– £8,000 – £32,000). Most candidates picked up the deduction for the director’s
remuneration, but the deduction for the pension contribution was generally overlooked.
Income tax: With a working at the margin approach , the income tax liability was simply
£8,000 at 45% = £3,600. The company pension contribution was an exempt benefit, and,
since it was paid by Zaoku Ltd, did not extend Kazuo’s tax bands as was often stated by
candidates.
NICs: With gross directors' remuneration of just £8,000, there were no class 1 NICs given
earnings were less than the lower threshold. Many candidates included the completely
separate salary of £200,000, and therefore calcul ated class 1 NICs at the rate of 2%. This is
why it is so important to read through the question carefully.
Comparison: When it came to the comparison with alternative 1, many candidates compared
the income tax and NICs, but forgot to include the corporation tax figures. This should have
been an easy one mark, as the mark was given provided a candidate made the comparison
using whatever figures they had calculated. Another common mistake was to make a
comparison based on a full computation approach with one done using a working at the
margin approach. It should have been apparent that such a tax difference was not realistic.
Many candidates wasted time by redoing their part (a) figures instead of just picking then up
from part (a).
Requirement (c) – 3 marks
There were a number of very good answers for this requirement. However, as already
mentioned, many candidates did not appreciate that part (c) was essentially the same as part
(a), but set a few years ahead with the dividend higher tax rate being applicable (rather than
the additional rate).
Full marks could have been obtained with the following working:
£31,900 (£40,000 – £7,600 – £500) at 5.6% (39.35% – 33.75%) = £1,786.
One fairly common mistake was to either ignore the corporation tax (which was unchanged)
or to calculate a new (and different) corporation tax figure.
The important thing when confronted by a different style of question to what has been
practiced (and this will often be the case with the higher skills questions) is to not panic, read
the question carefully to see what is required, and to appreciate that if workings become too
long or complicated, the requirement has not been properly understood.
🔑 Key Answer Tips

It is important to read the scenario and attempt each section of the requirement on its own,
making clear which tax you are calculating when a question tests multiple taxes. Alternative
1 does not have an impact on Alternative 2 and so on.
This is a higher skills question; hence it is essential to not waste time doing full computations
and work at the margin. Kazuo’s existing empl oyment will not change for Part (a) and (b).
That information is to assist you in determining the level of tax that will be applicable.
For part (c), the withdrawal of the income is a few years later when his other income is
reduced. This will impact the level of tax that is applicable. It is also important to identify that
the income from freelance work is only for one year (from 6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026). It is
not ongoing annual income.
(a) (i) Zaoku Ltd’s corporation tax liability for the year ended 5 April 2026 will be
£7,600 (£40,000 at 19%).
(ii) Kazuo will receivedividend income of £32,400 (£40,000 – £7,600) and the
income tax payable on this amount will be £12,553 ((£32,400 – £500) at 39.35%).

The rate of corporation tax will be 19% as the total taxable profits are less than the
lower limit of £50,000.
Dividend income will be taxed at the additional rate as Kazuo already has employment
income which makes him an additional rate taxpayer.
The first £500 of dividend income is taxed at 0% for all taxpayers.
(b) (i) 1 Paying the director’s remuneration and making the pension contribution
will reduce Zaoku Ltd’s taxable total profits (and corporation tax liability)
to £0 (£40,000 – £8,000 – £32,000).

Directors' remuneration and pension costs are allowable deductions for a company.
Therefore, the total taxable profits will be £Nil.
For Kazuo, the only taxable income will be the directors’ remuneration as the
contribution to the occupational pension scheme by the employer is an exempt benefit,
which is not subject to income tax or national insurance. When answering this part,
note that cash earnings are subject to class 1 NICs, however as the income was less
than the lower threshold, there are no NICs payable.
(c) 1 Zaoku Ltd’s corporation tax liability for the year ended 5 April 2026 will remain
unchanged at £7,600.

By the time Kazuo retires, he is a higher rate taxpayer as his income levels have changed
(he is now receiving pension income only). Therefore his dividend income from Zaoku
Ltd will be taxed at 33.75%.

towards the use of the property. Running costs totalling £850 for the tax year 2025/26

replaced washing machines which had been bought for £600 each in 2018. The

This question requires a full income tax computation, covering employment income with
various benefits and property income.
Remember to clearly classify income into non-savings, savings, and dividends, applying the

part of the basic or higher rate band.
Be meticulous with time-apportioning benefits and income where they do not apply for the
full tax year.
Ensure you distinguish between allowable and disallowable expenditure for property
income, particularly capital items, and consider the operation of replacement furniture relief.
Finally, always deduct PAYE from the overall tax liability.

📋 Examiner’s Report

The income tax question was based around Sheldon who was employed by Luqe Ltd.
This question was very well answered, with a number of perfect responses. However, quite
a few candidates failed to achieve fairly easy marks due to poor examination technique
and/or not reading the question carefully enough.
Although there were various ways of approaching this question, the easiest one was to have
a main computation with workings for employment income and for property income. Of
course, many candidates had a lot more workings than this, which would have taken more
time and made it more difficult to keep track of all the relevant figures.
As regards poor examination technique, one of the main problems here was not showing
workings. If workings are shown, marks will still be given even if an arithmetical mistake is
made. For example, one candidate incorrectly showed the beneficial loan as ((£80,000 –
£72,000)/2) × 3.75% × 8/12 = £100. The correct calculation was ((£80,000 + £72,000)/2) ×
3.75% × 8/12 = £1,900. However, because they had shown their workings, they were awarded
1 of the available 1.5 marks.
As regards not reading the question carefu lly enough, there were two quite common
mistakes made that were costly in terms of marks:
• Luqe Ltd provided Sheldon with living accommodation. Even though the question
stated that living accommodation was provided throughout the tax year, a number of
candidates misread the subsequent statement that Sheldon first moved into the
property on 1 January 2025. They took this to be the 1 January during the tax year in
question (which would have been 1 January 2026) and then restricted living
accommodation benefits by 3/12ths.
• For the property income expenses, it was stated that Sheldon’s expenditure was
£35,800 for the tax year. This figure included three amounts, only one of which was
disallowable (£1,600 for legal fees in relation to the grant of a five-year lease). The
deduction was therefore a quite straightforward £35,800 – £1,600 = £34,200.
However, many candidates either ignored the total figure of £35,800, deducted
£35,800 along with some or all the other fi gures, or deducted an adjusted version of
£35,800 along with some or all the other figures. There were two marks for the correct
deduction, but the incorrect variations scored poorly.
Candidates should avoid putting detailed workings within the one cell because it is too easy
to make a mistake with the syntax. Referring to the beneficial loan working again, one
mistake that cropped up several times was (£80,000 + £72,000/2) = £116,000 rather than the
correct ((£80,000 + £72,000)/2) = £76,000. Although candidates are not usually penalised for
such obvious errors, it will be an issue where more complicated workings are involved.
Candidates who rush their response, can sometime s fail to spot the obvious. Before taking
account of benefits or other income, Sheldon had a gross annual salary of £126,000. This
level of income by itself meant that Sheldon was not entitled to any personal allowance and
was an additional rate taxpayer. The personal allowance was sometimes given regardless,
and the tax rate applied to Sheldon’s dividend income was sometimes not 39.35%.
Looking at some of the other half marks on this question:
• The half mark for the use of Luqe Ltd’s company gym being an exempt benefit was
picked up by virtually every candidate.

• The half mark for the living accommodation running costs of £850 was sometimes not
given because this figure was deducted rather than treated as a benefit.
• The half mark for deducting the £3,000 (£250 × 12) that Sheldon paid towards the living
accommodation was sometimes not given because 12 months of payment were not
used.
• The half mark for the medical insurance benefit of £890 was sometimes not given due
to this incorrectly being treated as an exempt benefit.
• The half mark for the reimbursed business expenditure of £600 was sometimes not
given because this was either treated as taxable or deductible.
Not achieving a few half marks may not sound that serious, but if done a few times it can
easily be the difference between a marginal fail and a pass mark.

Q102 · KAGAN
+10 XPC · CONSTRUCTED
KAGAN
This scenario relates to four requirements.
You should assume that today’s date is 4 April 2025.
On 2 April 2025, Kagan inherited some quoted ordinary shares valued at £510,000 following
the death of his aunt. Kagan is unsure whether to retain the shares or sell some of them in
order to make some alternative investments.
Kagan is aged 61 and is an additional rate taxpayer. Prior to the inheritance, his taxable
income, consisting entirely of employment income, for the tax year 2025/26 would have
been £400,000. The income tax liability on this income for the tax year 2025/26 would have
been £166,203.
Prior to receiving the inheritance, Kagan’s chargeable estate for inheritance tax (IHT)
purposes was valued at £1,700,000. IHT of £550,000 would be payable were he to die in the
near future.
Retain the inherited shares
If Kagan simply retains the inherited shares, then he will receivedividend income of £15,300
during the tax year 2025/26. This is in addition to his employment income of £400,000.
Sell some inherited shares and make four alternative investments
Kagan is considering selling some of his inherited shares (for which there has only been a
minimal increase in value since he inherited them) to fund the following four investments, all
of which will be made at the start of the tax year 2025/26:
1 Kagan will make a gross personal pension co ntribution of £100,000. Kagan is a member
of a pension scheme, but has not made any contributions in recent years because his
income has been substantially lower than it is for the tax year 2025/26. He therefore
has sufficient unused annual allowances to cover a pension contribution of £100,000.
Kagan will immediately withdraw £25,000 of the pension fund tax-free. This is the
permitted tax-free amount. However, no pension will be taken during the tax year
2025/26.
2 Kagan will invest £50,000 in premium bonds. The expected amount of premium bond
prizes which will be received during the tax year 2025/26 is £700.
3 Kagan will invest the maximum permitted amount of £20,000 in a cash individual
savings account (ISA). The ISA will pay interest of £400 during the tax year 2025/26.
4 Kagan will purchase a freehold property for £295,000 (including all costs of purchase).
The property will be let out unfurnished, wi th Kagan receiving property income of
£9,600 during the tax year 2025/26.
After making these four investments, Kagan will be left with £65,000 of inherited shares, on
which he will receivedividend income of £450 during the tax year 2025/26. He will also have
his employment income of £400,000.

Students needed to be especially careful not to mix up the rules for IHT and CGT.

Tutorial notes

📋 Examiner’s Report

Part (a) for 1 mark required candidates to calc ulate Kagan’s revised income tax liability for
the tax year 2025/26 if he retained the inherited shares. Although fairly well answered, many
candidates used valuable time doing full before and after tax computations. Kagan was
clearly an additional rate taxpayer, so all that was required was to calculate the additional
rate tax due on the dividend income and then add it to the provided figure of tax on the
employment income.
Part (b)(i) for 1 mark required an explanation as to why little or no capital gains tax would
have been payable if Kagan had sold some of his inherited shares. This was because assets
are inherited at the value at the time of the deceased’s death. If these assets are sold soon
after being inherited, there will generally be a minimal increase in value (this fact was stated
in the question), so any gain is likely to be covered by the annual exempt amount. It was
pleasing to see that this part was well answered by those candidates who appreciated the
tax treatment. Part (b)(ii) for 6 marks required a calculation of Kagan’s revised income tax
liability for the tax year 2025/26 if he sold so me of his inherited shares and made the four
alternative investments. This section was re asonably well answered, but several points
should be noted:
The question stated that a full tax computation was required, so exempt items (pension lump
sum, premium bond prizes and the interest from the ISA) should simply have been listed
within the main computation and indicated as such by the use of zero (0) – not by an
explanation.
• The non-availability of the personal allowa nce should have been indicated in the same
manner. There was no need to justify the non-availability given the level of Kagan’s
income.
• Although there might only be a ½ mark av ailable for recognising an exemption, it is
important to know the various exemptions so that time is not spent producing
unnecessary, and more complicated workings – such as applying the savings income
nil rate band where the interest from the ISA was included as savings income.
Part (c) for 2 marks required candidates to state for each of the four alternative investments
whether the investment would reduce Kagan’s potential inheritance tax liability compared
to him retaining the inherited shares. Unfort unately, this section was not well answered.
Candidates need to remember, that unlike other taxes, there are few exemptions from
inheritance tax. Therefore, the replacement of the quoted shares with either premium
bonds, an ISA or freehold property would not have changed the value of Kagan’s chargeable
estate. However, the investment in the pension fund (which is not withdrawn) would have
been outside of Kagan’s estate, thereby reducing his potential IHT liability.

Q103 · ESME
+10 XPC · CONSTRUCTED
ESME
This scenario relates to three requirements.
Esme is employed by HHK plc. The following information is available for the tax year 2025/26:
(1) HHK plc paid Esme a gross annual salary of £45,000.
(2) During the tax year 2025/26, Esme received a bonus of £19,000 on 10 April 2025 and
another bonus of £22,000 on 22 March 2026. Esme was contractually entitled to
receive these bonuses on 31 March 2025 and 31 March 2026 respectively.

company car. The car has a list pric e of £42,000 and an official CO₂ emissions rate of
173 grams per kilometre. Esme was not provided with any fuel for private journeys.
(4) On 1 December 2025, Esme purchased her own car for £20,000. During the period
1 December 2025 to 5 April 2026, Esme drove a total of 23,000 miles, of which 12,000
were for business journeys. HHK plc reimbursed Esme £5,760 for the business
journeys.
(5) Esme contributed 4% of her gross annual salary of £45,000 into HHK plc’s occupational
pension scheme. HHK plc contributed a further 2% into the pension scheme on Esme’s
behalf.
Other information
(1) During the tax year 2025/26, Esme received dividend income of £6,000 from quoted
shares. Esme is considering transferring these shares to her husband, Andy.
(2) During the tax year 2025/26, Esme made a charitable donation of £5,000 (net) under
the gift aid scheme.

Esme’s husband
Esme is married to Andy. Andy’s only income in the tax year 2025/26 is dividend income of
£7,000.
Both Esme and Andy’s income is expected to remain the same for the foreseeable future.
Required:
(a) Calculate Esme’s income tax liability for the tax year 2025/26. 
Note: You should indicate by the use of zero (0) any items which are not taxable or
deductible. (10 marks)
(b) Explain how a married couple can reduce their income tax liabilities for the tax year
2025/26 by claiming the transferable amount of personal allowance (the marriage
allowance), and state why such a claim is not possible for Esme and Andy. 
(3 marks)
(c) Explain how both Esme's income tax liability and Andy’s income tax liability for the
tax year 2026/27 would be affected if they were to transfer all of the quoted shares
currently held by Esme to Andy. 
Notes:
1 You are not expected to recalculate all of Esme’s income tax liability.
2 You should assume that income tax rates and allowances remain unchanged.
(2 marks)
(Total: 15 marks)
✍️ Constructed response — attempt the full computation in your answer book, then compare with the official solution below.
103 ESME

5 April 2025 (the reimbursement by HHK plc resulted in a taxable benefit for the tax
year 2025/26):
• Contributions into HHK plc’s occupational pension scheme by both Esme and HHK plc
on Esme’s behalf (HHK plc’s contributions being an exempt benefit); and
• Esme making a charitable donation of £5,000 (net) under the gift aid scheme.
Candidates were instructed to indicate by the use of zero (0) any items which were not
taxable or deductible. In this case, the relevant items were the pension contributions made
by HHK plc and the first bonus.
There were no consistent mistakes made with this requirement, although the pension
contributions and charitable donation sometimes caused confusion. The correct treatment
was to deduct Esme’s pension contributions, ignore the contributions made by HHK plc, and
to extend the basic rate band by £6,250 (£5,000 × 100/80) for the charitable donation. As
already mentioned, question practice will help reinforce these basic principles.
Because of the dividend income, a two-column layout was most suitable for this requirement.
With any deductions included as negatives, it is then just a matter of using the SUM function
to get to the taxable income figures.
The only aspect of the answer which warranted a separate working was the mileage benefit.
Everything else was easily dealt with within the main computation.
Layout is not something candidates should really be concerned about on the day. With
sufficient question practice, the correct layout becomes automatic.
Requirement (b) was generally reasonably well answered, although many responses –
although correct – lacked sufficient detail to be awarded full marks.
When faced with this type of requirement, it is best to cover as many aspects as possible. So
here, it was necessary to show how the personal allowance of the transferor would be
reduced (£12,570 – £1,260 = £11,310) and ho w the transferee would benefit from a tax
reduction (£1,260 × 20% = £252). In both cases, the relevant figures, where provided by
candidates, assisted with their explanation.
The reason that a claim was not possible in Esme and Andy’s case was because Esme was a
higher rate taxpayer for the tax year 2025/26. This point was often not appreciated.
Requirement (c) often caused problems for candi dates, and it was not answered as well as
the other two requirements.
The starting point is to appreciate that all of Esme’s dividend income of £6,000 will move
from her to Andy. Based on the income tax workings from requirement (a), it is then a fairly
easy matter to establish the reduction to Esme’s income tax liability (£1,856 as per the
workings in requirement (a)).
Andy already had dividend income of £7,000, so the transfer of £6,000 will increase his
dividend income to £13,000. However, he will not have any income tax liability because of
the personal allowance (£12,570) and the dividend nil rate band of £500.

Part (a) of this question is a standard income tax computation, involving employment income

Part (b) requires an explanation of the tran sferable marriage allowance as well as an
explanation of why that is not relevant for Esme and Andy. Note that there are three marks
available here, so it is important to make three clear points.
Part (c) involves an inter spouse transfer of shares and the income tax implications of this. It
is important to consider the implications for both partners. Some clear guidance is provided
by the examiner in the requirement, so make sure you follow it!

by a maximum of £252 (£1,260 × 20%).

taxpayer.

shareholdings. If Esme’s quoted shares were transferred to Andy, his net income
would increase to £13,000 (£7,000 + £6,000). This would be partially relieved by
Andy’s personal allowance of £12,570 with the remainder covered by the
dividend nil rate band of £500.

£1,856.

Q104 · TONIE (ADAPTED)
+10 XPC · CONSTRUCTED
TONIE (ADAPTED)
This scenario relates to three requirements.
Up to and including the tax year 2023/24, Tonie was resident in the UK for tax purposes,
spending more than 300 days in the UK each year. Tonie understands that for the tax year
2025/26, she will again automatically be treated as resident in the UK, but is unsure of her
residence status for the tax year 2024/25. For this tax year, Tonie was neither automatically
resident in the UK nor automatically not resident. Throughout the tax year 2024/25, Tonie
was travelling around the world and did not stay in any one country for longer than 30 days,
although she did spend a total of 50 days in the UK. Tonie has a house in the UK, but it was
let out throughout the tax year 2024/25. She is single, has no children, and stayed with a
friend on the 50 days that she spent in the UK. Tonie did not do any substantive work in the
UK during the tax year 2024/25.
The following information is available for the tax year 2025/26:
Employment
On 6 April 2025, Tonie, who is a software de veloper, accepted a one-year contract to
maintain websites for Droid plc. Droid plc treated the contract as one of employment, with
the payments to Tonie being subject to PAYE. However, Tonie thought that, because she was
working from home, her employment status should instead have been one of self-
employment.

1 For the term of the contract, from 6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026, Tonie was paid a fixed
gross amount of £6,200 a month. During the term of the contract, Tonie was not
permitted to work for any other clients. She was required to do the work personally,
not being permitted to sub-contract the work to anyone else.
2 During the term of the contract, Tonie worked from home, but had to attend weekly
meetings at Droid plc’s offices to receiv e instructions regarding the work to be
performed during the following week. During the period 6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026,
Tonie used her private car for business visits to Droid plc’s clients. She drove 2,300
miles, for which Droid plc paid an allowance of 60 pence per mile.
3 During the term of the contract, Tonie leased computer equipment at a cost of £180 a
month. This was used 100% for business purposes.
Property income
1 Tonie owns a freehold house which is let out. The total amount of rent received during
the tax year 2025/26 was £10,080.
2 Tonie partly financed the purchase of the property with a repayment mortgage, paying
mortgage interest of £4,200 during the tax year 2025/26.
3 During May 2025, Tonie purchased a new washer-dryer for the property at a cost of
£640. This was a replacement for an old washing machine which was scrapped, with
nil proceeds. The cost of a similar washing machine would have been £380.
4 During November 2025, Tonie purchased a new dishwasher for the property at a cost
of £560. The property did not previously have a dishwasher.
5 The other expenditure on the property for the tax year 2025/26 amounted to £1,110,
and this is all allowable.
6 During the tax year 2025/26, Tonie rented out one furnished room of her main
residence. During the year, she received rent of £8,580 and incurred allowable
expenditure of £870 in respect of the room. Tonie always uses the most favourable
basis as regards the tax treatment of the furnished room.
Other income
1 On 1 July 2025, Tonie inherited £100,000 (nomin al value) of gilts paying interest at the
rate of 3%. The inheritance was valued at £120,000. Interest is paid half-yearly on
30 June and 31 December based on the nominal value. Tonie sold the gilts on
30 November 2025 for £121,250 (including accrued interest).
2 On 31 January 2026, Tonie received a premium bond prize of £100.
3 On 31 March 2026, Tonie received interest of £520 on the maturity of savings
certificates from NS&I (National Savings and Investments).
Required:
(a) Explain why Tonie was treated as not resident in the UK for the tax year 2024/25.

📋 Examiner’s Report

This question involved an individual who was planning to purchase a residential freehold
property which was going to be let out. She was unsure whether to purchase the property
personally or via a limited company. The limited company would be incorporated for the sole
purpose of purchasing and letting out the property, and Kat would hold all of the shares in
the company. The company’s corporation tax liability was provided in the question.
Part (a) for 9 marks required candidates to determine if there would be an overall saving of
tax if Kat purchased the property via a limited company rather than purchasing it personally.
Those candidates who made sure that they understood the scenario and worked carefully
through each calculation had no difficulty answering this section.
As warned in previous reports, where a tax figure is given for one of the scenarios (in this
case, the corporation tax figure), candidates sh ould never attempt to recalculate the figure
for themselves. All this does is use up valuable time. As regards the conclusion, this should
have just been a calculation of the tax difference between the two scenarios. There was no
need for a detailed explanation.
Where computations are required for two different scenarios, candidates should clearly
indicate which scenario is being answered. This is particularly important where some of the
same information is used in both scenarios. In this case employment income and the personal
allowance were common across both scenarios. Some candidates attempted to answer this
question with just the one computation; impossible given that property income formed part
of the first computation, with dividend income included in the second.
It should have been quite clear from the info rmation provided that full computations were
necessary for both scenarios. Those candidates who calculated the tax liability for a personal
purchase and then attempted to adjust the figures for a corporate purchase invariably ended
up with a very confused answer.
The personal purchase required candidates to apply the restriction whereby relief for 100%
of property income finance costs is restricted to the basic rate.
Working through past examination questions will help candidates familiarise themselves with
the best approach to be taken when answering questions which examine more than one tax.
Also, it is important that candidates appreciate the interactions that can arise in such
questions, and an article has been published covering many of the scenarios which could be
examined.
Part (b) for 1 mark required an explanation of one way in which the calculation of a future
taxable gain on a property disposal made by the limited company would differ from the
calculation of a taxable gain on a disposal made personally by Kat. Although there were many
good answers to this section, some candidate s discussed the finance costs restriction when
this has nothing to do with taxable gains. All that was required was a brief mention (not a
detailed answer) of the annual exempt amount.

📋 Examiner’s Report

The 10-mark higher skills question involved Be rtie, who was the managing director of, and
100% shareholder in, Rebite Ltd. Bertie had previously withdrawn a high level of director’s
remuneration from Rebite Ltd, but is considering more beneficial alternative arrangements
for the tax year 2025/26.
Existing arrangements: Bertie will be paid gross director’s remuneration of £75,000 and will
then use his private car for business mileage (b eing paid a mileage allowance for doing so).
He will make personal pension contributions of £25,000 (gross).
Beneficial arrangements: Instead of director’s remuneration, Bertie will be paid dividends of
£35,000. He will also be provided with an electric company car which will be leased by Rebite
Ltd. Instead of Bertie personally making personal pension contributions, Rebite Ltd will make
pension contributions of £25,000 into a company pension scheme on his behalf.
Provided candidates kept the two sets of information separate, this question as a whole was
generally very well answered. One particular problem however, was that some candidates
treated Rebite Ltd’s trading profit of £340,000 as personal income. Although the general
approach when marking is that candidates only lose marks once under the “own figure rule”,
having such a high level of income completely distorted the income tax calculations, with the
result that several half-marks were sometimes not able to be awarded.
With this style of question, it is very import ant to use appropriate headings so that it is
obvious which aspect of the requirement is being answered.

Although a higher skills question, candidates were instructed to produce full income tax and
NIC computations. Candidates seem to prefer this approach (compared to working at the
margin), and this largely explains the very good performance.
There were many perfect answers to both aspects of requirement (a).
Existing arrangements
In regard to the existing arrangements, a number of candidates did not appreciate that the
allowance received by Bertie for business mile age in his private car was tax-free with no
expense claim possible. This was because the a llowance of 45 pence per mile is exactly the
amount of authorised mileage allowance permitted by HM Revenue & Customs.
When it came to the income tax computation, a fairly common mistake was to not appreciate
that Bertie’s liability was solely at 20% given the extent that the basic rate band was extended
by his personal pension contributions.
With the calculation of employee class 1 NIC, quite a few candidates did not use Bertie’s gross
director’s remuneration of £75,000 as the limiting figure. Instead, the taxable income figure
was often used, or a figure adjusted for personal pension contributions and/or the mileage
allowance.
Beneficial arrangements
In regard to the beneficial arrangements, there were various mistakes:
• Normal tax rates were sometimes applied instead of the dividend tax rates;
• It was not appreciated that with just dividend income, there would be no NIC payable;
• The car benefit – although correctly calculated – was sometimes shown as separate to
the main income tax calculation (the basic rate of 20% was then applied, even though
the benefit was clearly covered by Bertie’s personal allowance); and
• Rebite Ltd’s pension contributions on Bertie’s behalf were taken into account despite
being an exempt benefit.
Again, there were many perfect answers to requirement (b).
One particular problem was that a number of candidates recalculated Rebite Ltd’s
corporation tax liability under the existing arrangements, despite being instructed not to do
so – this figure was being provided. If the correct figure was recalculated, this was just a case
of some time being wasted. However, an incorrect calculation meant both wasted time and
the inability to get the half-mark. This is why it is so important to read through the question
carefully, especially the requirements along with any guidance notes.
The computation itself was fairly straightforward, and half the marks would have been given
if just the trading profit of £340,000 was taxed at 25%, with this figure then compared to the
given corporation tax liability under the existing arrangements. To get full marks, it was also
necessary to deduct the leasing costs and the pension contributions.
The dividends paid to Bertie were irrelevant, although some candidates insisted on deducting
them. This is why question practice is so important because this is the type of mistake which
when made once, candidates learn not to repeat.

📋 Examiner’s Report

The 10-mark higher skills question involved Afia, Afua and Akua who had been in partnership
since 6 April 2011. The partners were considering incorporating the partnership’s business
on 6 April 2025; the new limited company to be called Triple A Ltd.
With this type of question, it is very important that candidates read the question and
requirements carefully, and to note which tax figures have been provided to them. In this
case, they were given the total income tax liab ilities and NICs (for all three partners) if the
partners continued to trade as a partnership. They were also provided with the total amount
of class 1 employee and employer NICs in respect of the director’s remuneration to be paid
by Triple A Ltd. A number of candidates, however, wasted time by calculating NIC figures.
Overall, this question was reasonably well answered. Those candidates who tried to use the
provided partners’ income tax figure as a ba sis for calculating the income tax payable by
directors, invariably did not achieve a pass mark.
A surprising number of candidates had difficulty, despite a very similar example being
available in the higher skills article. It is im portant to appreciate the interactions that can
arise in a higher skills question, and reading published articles and practising exam standard
questions will help to this end.
Requirement (i)
This was a very straightforward computation provided candidates ignored the pension
contributions made by Triple A Ltd, and used the correct rate of tax for the dividend income.
There was a mark for knowing that the pension contributions were exempt, but this was only
given if this point was indicated by either a zero entry or an explanation. Many candidates
did not do this, thereby missing the very easy mark.

Because all three directors had the same income, the correct approach was to do the one
income tax calculation and to then multiply the end result by three. Quite a number of
candidates wasted time (even if it was just a matter of copy and paste) by producing three
separate, but exactly the same, computations.
Requirement (ii)
The corporation tax working for Triple A Ltd was somewhat more difficult, although there
were a number of perfect answers.
Candidates had to start with the company’s taxable total profits (figure provided), then
deduct the total director’s remuneration, class 1 employer NICs and pension scheme
contributions (all these figures were provided). It was necessary, however, to multiply the
provided figures for director’s remuneration and pension scheme contributions by three –
the number of directors.
Dividends should be ignored, although quite a few candidates deducted them.
Another mistake sometimes made was to deduct the class 1 employee NICs as well as, or
instead of, the employer NICs. If this was done, the half mark for correctly deducting just the
employer NICs was not given.
Provided the correct figures were deducted, candidates would then have had a revised
taxable total profits figure of below £50,000. The corporation tax calculation was therefore
at the single rate of 19%.
If any of the figures were missed, candidates would have been faced with a more difficult
marginal relief calculation for equivalent marks. With no dividend income, this could have of
course been calculated as £50,000 at 19%, with the balance of profits charged at 26.5%.
Requirement (iii)
The comparison meant pulling to gether figures from both the scenario as well as ones
calculated.
The comparison was between the total tax and NIC liabilities for the partners if they had
continued to trade as a partnership (these figures were all provided) and the total income
tax liabilities of the directors (calculated), the corporation tax liability of Triple A Ltd
(calculated) and the class 1 employee and employer NICs (figures provided).
Most candidates achieved at least some marks here, with many gaining the full 1.5 marks.
The most common mistake was to omit the corporation tax payable by Triple A Ltd.

Capital allowances on car purchases are calculated based on the CO₂ emissions.
As the car purchased in this question has CO₂ emissions of between 1 – 50 grams per
kilometre, it is eligible for a WDA at 18%. The WDA then needs to be adjusted for the private
use by Idris, as only the business use proportion of the allowance can be claimed.
The business mileage is 13,000 out of 20,000 miles (i.e. 65%).


(b) Taxable trading profit – Cash basis

When operating the cash basis adjustments need to be made for any revenue not received or
purchases not actually paid for during the year (i.e. receivables and payables).
The car expenses deduction is calculated using the HMRC approved mileage allowances. The
private use of business premises flat rate adjus tment covers the private use of food, utilities
and other household goods and services.
Capital purchases are deductible in full in the year of purchase; however, no deduction is
available for the purchase of a car as this is covered by the approved mileage allowance.

ETHEL Walk in the footsteps of a top tutor
This scenario relates to two requirements.
Ethel Brown started to run a small bed and breakfast business as a sole trader on 6 April 2025.
She prepared her first accounts for the year to 5 April 2026.
She has read about the cash basis of accounting and HMRC flat rate expense adjustments
which are intended to simplify tax accounting for small businesses.
In the year to 5 April 2026 she has the following transactions:
1 Ethel earned income of £74,500 during the year. At 5 April 2026 £10,000 of the income
was still outstanding.
2 Payments of £25,000 in respect of food, utilities and other household costs. She lives
in part of the bed and breakfast premises with her husband and two children and 35%
of the food, utilities and other household costs relate to their private use. The HMRC
flat rate private use adjustment for four occupants of business premises is £7,800.

3 On 1 June 2025 Ethel paid a car dealer £14,000 by cheque for a car with CO₂ emissions
of 40 grams per kilometre. She also made payments totalling £3,000 related to the
running costs of the car for the year. She has used the car 40% of the time for private
purposes and she drove 11,000 business miles during the year.
4 On 1 March 2026 she acquired an item of kitchen equipment for £350 on credit terms.
She paid the supplier’s invoice on 15 April 2026.
Required:
(a) Calculate Ethel’s taxable trading profit for the year ended 5 April 2026 assuming that
she prepares her accounts using the cash basis and opts to use the HMRC flat rate
expense adjustments for both the car and the private use of the business premises.
Your answer should be supported with brief notes to explain how you have treated
the transactions in Notes 1 to 4.

You should ignore VAT. (6 marks)
(b) Calculate Ethel’s tax adjusted trading profit for the year ended 5 April 2026 assuming
that she elects to prepare her accounts using the accruals basis. 
You should ignore VAT. (4 marks)
(Total: 10 marks)

109 ETHEL Walk in the footsteps of a top tutor

1 Income
• The income of £10,000 outstanding at the year-end is excluded when
calculating the profit using the cash basis. When using cash accounting,
income is only included if it has been received during the period.

2 Business premises used partly for private purposes
• The total payments of £25,000 can be deducted from the trading profit
but the flat rate private use adjustment of £7,800 must be added to the
trading profit for tax purposes.
• A net deduction from trading profits of £17,200 can therefore be claimed
for tax purposes.
3 Car used for private and business purposes
• The cash payments in respect of the purchase and running costs of the car
totalling £17,000 (£14,000 + £3,000) are not deductible from the trading
profit and capital allowances are not available as she is using HMRC’s
approved mileage allowances.
• The tax deduction for the car is allowed using the approved mileage
allowances for the business mileage as follows:

–––––

–––––
4 Kitchen equipment
• A tax deduction can be claimed from the trading profits for the full cost of
the kitchen equipment when the invoice is paid.
• No tax deduction is therefore allowed in the accounts for the year to
5 April 2026 but Ethel will obtain a tax deduction of £350 from trading
profits in the following year to 5 April 2027.

Tutorial notes
1 The question states that Ethel uses the cash basis and opts to use the flat rate expense
adjustments.
2 Where a business premises is used partly for private purposes (e.g. a bed and breakfast
or small care home), a private use adjustment must be made for tax purposes if the full
cost of food, utilities and other household goods have been included in the accounts.
The HMRC flat rate private use adjustments are based on the number of occupants and
will be provided as part of the question in the examination. Any information regarding
actual private expenses is irrelevant.
3 The flat rate expense adjustment in respect of cars is based on the HMRC approved
mileage allowances. These are the same rates that are used to calculate the taxable
benefit/allowable deduction where employees use their own cars for business
purposes. The rates are given in the tax tables provided in the examination.
4 Under the cash basis a 100% trading deduction is given for the acquisition cost of items
of plant and machinery (other than cars) rather than capital allowances.

This question includes an adjustment of profits and then an income tax computation
incorporating the trading profit, employment income, a premium bond prize and interest
income. It finally ends with a question on payrolling benefits.
When calculating tax adjusted trading profit, remember to account for private use
adjustments and to correctly calculate capital allowances, especially for short-life assets and
cars with private use.
For taxable income, carefully distinguish between taxable and exempt income and make sure
you show the income which is exempt in your answer to be awarded with half a mark. Ensure
to deduct allowable employment expenses and carefully consider the treatment of items like
clothing for work.
Finally, there are two marks available for statin g the advantages of payrolling benefits. In
order to be awarded the two marks, two distinct points must be made.
