177 GINGER AND NIGEL (ADAPTED) Walk in the footsteps of a top tutor

1 A disposal by Innocent will qualify for BADR as she is the managing director of
Cinnamon Ltd, the company is a trading company, her shareholding of 20%
(20,000/100,000) is more than the minimum required holding of 5% and she has held
the shares and worked for the company for more than two years. The gain is therefore
taxed at 14%.
2 A disposal by Nigel will not qualify for BADR as he is not an officer or an employee of
Cinnamon Ltd and his shareholding is only 3% (3,000/100,000). As Nigel is a higher rate
taxpayer (taxable income £80,000) the gain is taxed at the higher rate of 24%.
3 A disposal by Nigel will not qualify for investors’ relief as he did not subscribe for the
shares (i.e. buy newly issued shares from the company).

This question tests two important capital gains tax reliefs: gift holdover relief and BADR.
Part (a) tested gift holdover relief but in a slightly unusual way which required the application
of the modified gift holdover relief rules for sales at an undervaluation, and a calculation of
the maximum number of shares that can be gifted without a capital gains tax liability arising.
If you are ever unsure of how to deal with part of a question, it is important to make a sensible
attempt and move on, rather than waste time, or potentially miss easy marks by not
attempting to answer the part.
The highlighted words are key words or phrases that markers are looking for.
Part (b) compares the CGT payable by a husband or wife on the disposal of shares. Again,
easy marks were available for the basic capital gains tax computation in each case and the
calculation of the difference in tax payable by the two individuals.

(a) Ginger

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

Remember that where there is a disposal at an undervalue (as opposed to an outright gift)
then part of the gain may be chargeable now and cannot be held over (deferred).
The examining team has given you a hint in the question as to how to approach the answer
by stating that Ginger has not utilised her annual exempt amount.
• The disposal is at an undervalue, so only the ‘gift’ element of the gain can be
held over.
• The consideration paid for each share w ill be immediately chargeable to capital
gains tax to the extent that it exceeds the allowable cost.
• The chargeable amount is therefore £1.61 (£4.00 – £2.39) per share.
• Ginger’s annual exempt amount fo r the tax year 2025/26 is £3,000.
• She can therefore sell 1,863 shares (£3,000/£1.61) to her daughter without this
resulting in any capital gains tax liability for the tax year 2025/26.

This method may have proved quite challenging to some students. If you are unsure how to
tackle the question, then make sure you write down what you do know.
One mark was available for simply stating how to calculate the gain on a transfer at an
undervalue and another half mark for stating the amount of the annual exempt amount!

should give you a hint that you should consider how this is relevant for determining their CGT

(b) Inheritance tax
Inheritance tax is charged on a transfer of value of chargeable property by a chargeable
person. A transfer of value is a gift of any asset which results in a reduction in value of
the donor’s estate.
Daljeet is going to sell either the ABC Ltd shares, or the holiday cottage at arm’s length
and receive consideration in return. He does not intend to make a gift of either asset,
so there is no transfer of value for inheritance tax purposes.

179 LUNA LTD Walk in the footsteps of a top tutor
🔑 Key Answer Tips

As this question concerns chargeable gains for companies, be careful to ensure that your
answer does not refer to individuals, an annual exempt amount or capital gains tax.
A company pays corporation tax on its net char geable gains and there is no annual exempt
amount available for companies.
Part (a) is a deceptively straightforward written part about the indexation allowance and the
fact that it cannot create nor increase a capital loss.
The highlighted words in the answer are the key phrases that markers are looking for.
Part (b) requires two calculations in relation to share disposals, which could be attempted in
either order.
The first is a straightforward share disposal but potentially time consuming.
The second is more demanding and involves a takeover with mixed consideration, and a gain
arising in respect of the cash received.
(a) Indexation allowance

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

The requirement for part (a) is split into two parts so make sure your answer clearly sets out
your explanation for each part separately.
• Where a company makes a capital loss, then no indexation allowance is available
because it cannot be used to increase a loss.
• Where the indexation allowance is greater than a company’s unindexed gain,
then the gain is simply reduced to nil because the allowance cannot be used to
create a loss.
(b) Chargeable gains – year ended 31 March 2026

In the absence of guidance on the split of marks you should assume equal weighting is given
between the two disposals, and allocate your time accordingly.
It would be easy to spend too long on the first calculation you choose to tackle and miss easy
marks on the second.

The gift to Mario’s wife is exempt as the inter-spouse exemption applies.
The gift into the trust is a chargeable lifetime transfer and is therefore not exempt.
A lifetime transfer up to £5,000 given from pare nt to child on the occasion of the child’s
marriage is exempt, so the gift of £2,000 to Mario’s son is exempt.
The gift to Mario’s daughter is more than £250 and therefore the small gifts exemption does
not apply.

all available exemptions:
£

5 May 2017 Cash to his daughter 200,000
12 July 2021 An antique painting to his son 370,000
What is the amount of the nil rate band available in calculating the additional IHT due on
the gift of the antique painting as a result of Gabe's death?
✅ Answer: £325,000
182 £325,000
Both of Gabe’s lifetime gifts are PETs, which are not taxable and will not use any NRB during
his lifetime and will become exempt if he lives for seven years following the date of the gift.
Seven years prior to his death was 22 November 2018, and since the cash gift to his daughter
is before this date it will never become chargeable to IHT and is now exempt.
The gift of the painting to his son (£370,000) is within this seven-year period and becomes
chargeable using the nil rate band at death (£325,000). In the seven years prior to that gift
(12 July 2014 to 12 July 2021) the only gift was the PET to his daughter, which is now exempt,
so it does not use any NRB at death.
Therefore, the NRB available to the second PET on Gabe’s death is the full £325,000.
💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

Note that if the first gift had been a chargeable lifetime transfer (CLT), it would have used
some NRB on Gabe’s death.

+10 XPA · MCQ

On 1 July 2024, Sameer made a cash gift of £2,500 to his sister.

On 1 June 2025, he made a cash gift of £50,000 to a trust.

for inheritance tax purposes after taking account of all available exemptions?

£
✅ Answer: A
183 A
£
Transfer of value 50,000
Annual exemption
– 2025/26 (£3,000 – £2,000) (1,000)
– 2024/25 (£3,000 – £2,500) (500)
––––––
Gross chargeable transfer 48,500
––––––
💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

The annual exemption is set against PETs, even if they never become chargeable. The annual
exemption is offset against the earliest gift in the tax year automatically. The 2025/26 annual
exemption is therefore reduced by the amount given to Sameer’s friend, as this was before
the gift to the trust.
The current year’s annual exemption must be offset prior to the offset of any brought forward
amounts.
Any unused amounts can be carried forward one tax year, so the remaining annual exemption
from 2024/25 can also be offset.

Q185 · Question 185
+10 XPA · MCQ
185 September 2015 OT question
Heng is a wealthy 45 year old who would like to reduce the potential inheritance tax liability
on her estate when she dies.
Which of the following actions will NOT achieve Heng’s aim of reducing the potential
inheritance tax liability on her estate when she dies?
grandchildren rather than her children
rather than her children
✅ Answer: A
💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

Option A describes the common inheritance tax planning technique of ‘skipping a generation’.
This technique can maximise the inheritance available to future generations as a charge to
inheritance tax will only arise once, on th e passing of the estate residue to Heng’s
grandchildren. If the residue had been left to Heng’s children and they subsequently gifted
the assets to their children, two charges to inheritance tax would arise.
That being said, skipping a generation woul d not reduce Heng’s potential inheritance tax
liability on death as legacies left to both children and grandchildren are equally chargeable.

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

Repayment and interest-only mortgages are deductible.
Gambling debts owed to a friend are not legally enforceable and therefore not deductible. If
the gambling debt was legally enforceable then it would be deductible.
A verbal promise to pay a friend’s debt is not legally enforceable and therefore not deductible.
Funeral expenses and credit card debts are deductible.

200 D
Liability for payment
Trustees of the trust Sandeep
Due date
30 April 2026

📋 Examiner’s Report

This question tested candidates’ knowledge of the payment of IHT on a chargeable lifetime
transfer (CLT) to a trust. The donor, Sandeep, is primarily liable for the tax due on a CLT and
the due date is the later of the following:
(i) Six months after the end of the month of transfer
(ii) 30 April after the end of the tax year of transfer
The later of these dates is therefore 31 May 2026 and so the correct answer was D. Many
candidates were able to select the correct date, but were less successful in determining who
was primarily liable for payment. Tax administration and the payment of tax are important
aspects of the syllabus and candidates are reminded to devote sufficient attention to these
topics when preparing for the TX UK exam.

🔑 Key Answer Tips

This is a typical IHT question covering various aspects of lifetime gifts and then the death
estate. The question doesn’t test any peripheral topics and therefore should be relatively
straightforward.

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

The AE:
– exempts the first £3,000 of lifetime transfers in any one tax year
– is applied chronologically to the first gift in the tax year, then (if there is any left) the
second gift and so on
– must be applied to the first gift each year, even if the first gift is a PET and never
becomes chargeable.
Any unused AE can only be carried forward one tax year.

Gambling winnings and wasting chattels (e.g. a racehorse) are exempt assets for the purposes
of capital gains tax. It is common for these types of assets to be included in a death estate in
an examination question to test if you have remembered that there are no exempt assets for
inheritance tax. Therefore, it is important that you have a clear understanding of what assets
or income are exempt for each tax!
Note that the RNRB is applied to the entire estate not the main residence, so the value needed
here is the market value of £875,000 less the outstanding repayment mortgage of £500,000.

There is no nil rate band remaining as the gross chargeable transfer on 20 February 2019,
which is within the seven years before death, is greater than £325,000.
Tom is leaving his main residence to his children, therefore the additional residence nil rate
band of £175,000 is available to deduct from the estate. Note that this is not reduced by gross
chargeable transfers in the seven years before death.

🔑 Key Answer Tips

This IHT question starts by looking at two lifetime gifts, (one PET and one CLT). It then moves
on to consider what is included in the death estate. The last two questions cover the transfer
of the unused nil rate band from the spouse and the due dates of lifetime tax and tax on the
death estate.

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

The loss to the donor (or diminution in value) principle applies when calculating the transfer
of value for IHT purposes. This is particularly relevant when valuing shares where a majority
shareholding has a higher value per share than a minority shareholding in a company.
The transfer of value is the amount by which Afiya’s estate has diminished and not the market
value of the asset gifted.
Prior to the transfer Afiya had 8,000 shares (an 80% (8,000/10,000) shareholding) in the
company and the shares are valued at £8 per share.
After the transfer Afiya owns 1,500 shares (a 15% shareholding) and the shares are valued at
£3 per share.

When calculating lifetime tax on a CLT, the available nil rate band is reduced by the value of
CLTs in the previous seven years. PETs are ignored for lifetime tax calculations even if they
subsequently become chargeable.

Debts are only deductible if they were outstanding at the date of death and were imposed by
law.
The £500 owed to a friend is not a debt imposed by law, and so will not be deductible.
The annual exemption is only available for deduction from lifetime gifts in the calculation of
lifetime tax. They cannot, therefore, be deducted from the death estate.

The husband did not leave a main residence to direct descendants on his death so 100% of his
residence nil rate band (RNRB) is unused and could be transferred to Afiya. Note that the
husband does not need to have died after 5 April 2017 for the RNRB to be transferred to the
surviving spouse.

As the lifetime gift was made between 1 October and 5 April in the tax year 2024/25, the due
date for the lifetime IHT on the CLT to the trust is 31 July 2025, being six months from the end
of the month in which the gift was made.
The due date for the IHT on the estate is 31 May 2026, being six months after the end of the
month in which Afiya died.

🔑 Key Answer Tips

This question involves the IHT implications of gifts made by two individuals, both during their
lifetime and on death. It includes the calculation of death tax on a CLT, diminution in value
for share gifts, the small gifts exemption, and the IHT payable on their respective estates,
including the transferable nil rate band.
There is also one administration question covering who is responsible for paying the IHT on
a CLT and the tax due date. These administration questions result in easy marks if you know
the rules.

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

The annual exemption for the tax year 2022/23 had already been utilised by the PET to
Roman’s daughter on 4 March 2023.
The PET also reduced the available nil rate band for the gift to the trust. The transfer of value
in respect of the PET would be reduced by the 2021/22 and 2022/23 annual exemptions,
resulting in a chargeable amount of £204,000 (£210,000 – £6,000).

The trustees of the trust are responsible for paying the IHT arising on the trust on death. The
IHT is due to be paid six months from the end of the month of death.

The fall in the value of the donor’s estate must be calculated in order to determine the value
of the gift for IHT purposes. Paris had a 40% shareholding (100,000/250,000) prior to making
the gift and a 10% shareholding (25,000/250,000) after making the gift.
The rule is different to capital gains tax where the value of a 30% shareholding in isolation
would be used as the value of the gift in the computation.

Gifts of up to £250 per recipient per tax year are exempt from IHT under the small gifts
exemption. Accordingly, the gift of £210 is the only gift eligible for the small gift exemption.
The gifts of £80 and £195 are made to the same friend and must be considered in total when
determining whether the small gifts exemption applies.
The gifts that don’t qualify = £80 + £195 + £460 = £735

🔑 Key Answer Tips

This question focuses on various aspects of IHT, including the calculation of the nil rate band,
deductible liabilities, payment responsibilities, and tax planning implications of lifetime
transfers.
When calculating the available nil rate band, remember to consider any transferable nil rate
band from a deceased spouse. It's crucial to apply the rules for deductible liabilities
accurately and understand how previous gifts and unused nil rate bands affect the IHT
calculation on the death estate.
Pay close attention to who is responsible for paying IHT on the death estate and the specific
due dates for such payments. Finally, when evaluating the tax savings from lifetime gifts,
compare the IHT that would have been payable if the assets were retained until death against
the actual lifetime IHT paid and any IHT still due on death as a result of the gift.

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

The unused percentage (rather than amount) of nil rate band on the death of the first spouse
is applied to the nil rate band at the date of the death of the second spouse to determine the
additional amount of nil rate band available.
2
Deductible

The legal fees are not deductible as the debt is not legally enforceable.
Interest-only mortgages are allowable deductions.
Outstanding taxes such as income tax and capital gains tax can be deducted in the estate,
although the IHT itself is not deductible.

The personal representatives (executors) of the donor’s estate are responsible for paying any
IHT on the death estate and the IHT must be paid within six months from the end of the month
of death.

The assets would still have been subject to inheritance tax; therefore, no tax would have been
saved.
Assets left to a spouse are exempt from inheritance tax but assets left to other beneficiaries
are taxable as normal.

This IHT question starts by covering the death tax on a lifetime gift.
It then looks at the death estate, and how much inheritance is received by the residuary
legatee as well as the impact of leaving assets to a later generation.
Question four tests the comparison of lifetime giving rather than keeping an asset in the
death estate.
Finally, the question tests the administration rules regarding who has to pay the tax and
when. This provides an easy two marks if the administration rules for inheritance tax have
been learnt.

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

Note the PET in February 2017 has not used any NRB since there was no lifetime charge (being
a PET) and no charge on death (as it falls out of the seven year period).

It can be beneficial to skip a generation, i.e. leaving part of the estate to Marguerite’s children.
This avoids a further charge to IHT when the first generation (Marguerite) dies. Gifts will then
only be taxed once before being inherited by the second generation, rather than twice.

Death tax on lifetime gifts made by the deceased individual is paid by the recipient of
the gift. Thus, it is payable by the Grandson . It is due six months from the end of the
month of death, the end of the month of death was 30 June 2025 and therefore six
months after this is 31 December 2025.
Death tax is payable by the executors of the estate only on the estate left by the
deceased individual.

This IHT question starts with a calculation of the gross chargeable transfer on a chargeable
lifetime gift.
The second question tests the diminution in value principle in relation to the valuation of a
gift of shares.
The final three questions all relate to the same gift in different ways. The first asks for the
value of the exemptions which were available on the gift (note that these have already been
deducted in the transfer figure given in the question), the second asks for the inheritance tax
payable on the gift on death. Finally, the question tests the administration rules regarding
who has to pay the tax and when. This provides an easy two marks if the administration rules
for inheritance tax have been learnt.

The gross chargeable transfer is the value of the gift (after exemptions) plus the tax paid.

📋 Examiner’s Report

As is typical for the 10-mark question, different taxes were covered, in this case namely
inheritance tax and capital gains tax. The question revolved around three residential
properties owned by Aurora, with two of the properties qualifying for private residence relief.
The question was not particularly technical, and much of the relevant information was
provided. However, it was important for candidates to sort out which information related to
which requirement.
• As regards inheritance tax, it was the valu es of the three properties, the amount of
outstanding interest-only mortgages, and Aurora’s main residence.
• As regards capital gains tax, it was the chargeable gains, periods of ownership and the
periods which Aurora had lived in each property.
The 10-mark question will often exclude certain reliefs. This was the case here, with both
Aurora and her deceased husba nd, Andrew, having made lifetime gifts which fully utilised
their respective inheritance tax nil rate bands of £325,000. This being the case, the nil rate
bands could simply be ignored. Only the residence nil rate bands were relevant.
The capital gains tax requirement stated that the chargeable gain should be calculated before
deducting the annual exempt amount. Therefor e, the annual exempt amount and the tax
liability were irrelevant, and could not possibly gain any marks.
With the 10-mark question, it is always a good idea for candidates to spend a few minutes
planning out their answers, especially as this can avoid wasting time taking a much longer
approach than necessary. With this requirement, the three property values and the two
mortgage figures can be combined into just the two figures – £1,050,000 (3 × £350,000 for
the property values) and £230,000 (2 × £115,000 for the mortgages). Three separate sets of
workings not only take longer, but there is more scope for error.
The next important point is that the chargeable gain figures are completely irrelevant to this
requirement, and, as already noted, so are the nil rate bands of £325,000. It is also necessary
to include the main residence valued at £500,000. This is why the reading and planning aspect
of answering the 10-mark question is so important.
The only slightly technical aspect to the requi rement is the residenc e nil rate bands. Since
Andrew is deceased and would not have used his residence nil rate band on his death (the
entire estate being left to Aurora), two residence nil rate bands of £175,000 are available.
The total of £350,000 is clearly less than the value of the main residence (£500,000). As can
be seen from the model answer, all of this is easily combined into a computation with no
separate workings required.
Note: The question has been amended since it was originally set. Part of the examiner’s
report has been removed as it relates to a part of the question that has been deleted.
Requirement (b) – 3 marks
At just 3 marks, another short set of workings is required here.
Since the chargeable gains are given, it is just a matter of establishing the available reliefs. As
for requirement (a), it is important to ignore any information which is not relevant, such as
the property values and the mortgages.
There is a slightly more difficult aspect to this requirement:
• Although the periods of occupation are given, it is necessary to add in a further
9 months (0.75 years) where relevant for the final periods of ownership.
Note that the examiner’s comments regarding letting relief are no longer relevant due to
changes in the tax rules and have been deleted. This part of the question has been amended
to take into account the new rules.
The periods of ownership and the periods which Aurora has lived in each property are given
in years, so it makes sense to retain this format and not convert to months. The final 9 months
are simply included as 0.75 years.

🔑 Key Answer Tips

Part (a) for six marks was a standard IHT question requiring the calculation of the tax payable
on two lifetime gifts and the death estate as a result of the donor’s death. This part also
tested the knowledge of who is responsible for making the payments of IHT on both the
lifetime gifts and the death estate.
Parts (b) and (c) involved basic IHT planning – this had to be applied to the scenario.

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

The focus of this question was on lifetime gifts. Don’t be put off by the fact there are three
lifetime gifts made by the donor in the question.
Inheritance tax requires you to deal with the gifts in chronological order. Start with the
earliest gift and apply any available exemptions . You can then consider which gifts will be
subject to inheritance tax on the donor’s death; any gifts more than seven years prior to the
donor’s death will not be subject to IHT on death.
(a) James – Inheritance tax arising on death

The gift in October 2018 was made more t han seven years before the donor’s death and as
such there was no IHT due as a result of James’ death. This was a gift into a trust however,
which means it was chargeable to IHT immediately. As this gift was within seven years of the
next two lifetime gifts, the nil rate band available to these gifts is reduced accordingly.
(b) Skipping a generation avoids a further charge to inheritance tax when his brother dies.
Gifts will then only be taxed once before being inherited by his nephew, rather than
twice.
(c) 1 Even if the donor does not survive for seven years, taper relief will reduce the
amount of IHT payable after three years.

📋 Examiner’s Report

This question was on inheritance tax (IHT), and candidates found this to be a challenging area.
The requirement for part (a) was to calculate the IHT payable as a result of a taxpayer’s death,
and to state who was responsible for paying the tax. The taxpayer had made (1) a chargeable
lifetime transfer (more than seven years before death), (2) a potentially exempt transfer and
(3) another chargeable lifetime transfer. A quick review of the information given should have
indicated that no lifetime tax would have been paid (this fact was actually stated in respect
of the second chargeable lifetime transfer) and that taper relief was not relevant (given that
none of the gifts were between four and seven years of death). However, many candidates
dedicated a lot of time to establishing this. Candidates should read through the question
carefully before they begin their calculations.
Part (b) required an explanation as to why it might have been beneficial if the taxpayer had
left a portion of their estate to his nephew rather than to his brother. This aspect was well
answered, with most candidates appreciating the basic IHT planning of avoiding a double
charge to tax.
The IHT planning in part (c) was less well understood. It was necessary to explain why it might
be advantageous to make lifetime gifts even when such gifts are made within seven years of
death. The main advantage here is that the value of the gift is fixed at the time it is made, so
no IHT is payable on the increase in value between making the gift and the time of death.
Taper relief may also be available.

🔑 Key Answer Tips

This question requires the calculation of CGT and IHT on gifts made to a trust, as well as the
income tax implications of these gifts. It can be daunting when multiple taxes are covered in
one question, however the requirements are completely distinct and the income tax
information is separate in the question.
The challenge is therefore to distinguish the information needed for CGT and IHT and to
correctly apply the rules for valuing unquoted shares for IHT purposes and the CGT rules for
gifts. For the capital gains tax calculation, pay close attention to how the market value of
unquoted shares is determined. When calculating the lifetime inheritance tax, remember the
'loss to the donor' (diminution in value) principle. Also ensure you use the correct IHT rates
for lifetime transfers.
Finally, for the income tax reduction, focus on the change in Jessica's taxable income
categories due to the gifts. In order to calculate the answers in the time allowed for just three
marks, it will be necessary to work in the margin, rather than producing full income tax
computations. Make sure to apply the correct tax rates for savings and dividends for an
additional rate taxpayer.

Tutorial notes

📋 Examiner’s Report

The 10-mark higher skills question involved Jess ica, an additional rate taxpayer. On 6 April
2025, she had made a lifetime gift consisting of both shares and cash to a trust, with the
funds then being held for the benefit of her two grandchildren aged three and four.
Although this question was well answered, the fact that the same share information had to
be used for both capital gains tax and inheritance tax purposes often caused confusion. This
is despite a similar example being included in the higher skills, chargeable gains and
inheritance tax articles. It is important to appreciate the interactions that can arise in a higher
skills question, and reading publis hed articles and practising exam standard questions will
help to this end.
Requirement (a)
The relevant information to pull out from the question is that Jessica made a gift of 100,000
£1 ordinary shares in Valuable Ltd to the trust. With Valuable Ltd having a share capital of
250,000 £1 ordinary shares, the gift represents a 40% shareholding, so the relevant deemed
proceeds figure is based on £4 per share. The shares were acquired at a £1 par value.
Therefore, the gain is simply 100,000 × £3 (£4 – £1) = £300,000 (for 2 marks). Deduct the
annual exempt amount, multiply by the higher capital gains tax rate (since Jessica is an
additional rate taxpayer), and that gives the capital gains tax figure.
Provided the valuation basis is understood, that should be a very easy and quick 3 marks.
The big problem for many candidates, of course, was that they used an inheritance tax basis
of valuation. A common error was to calculate the inheritance tax value (£900,000 – part (b))
and then deduct the correct cost figure of £100,000 (100,000 at £1). This would have wasted
a minute or two on the erroneous calculation.
Requirement (b)
The diminution in value of Jessica’s estate wa s a cash element of £250,000 (for one mark),
and the 100,000 £1 ordinary shares in Valuab le Ltd. Before the transfer, Jessica owned
150,000 shares; a 60% shareholding valued at £7 per share. After the transfer, Jessica owned
50,000 shares; a 20% shareholding valued at £3 per share. The diminution in value from the
gift of shares was therefore (150,000 at £7) – (50,000 at £3) = £900,000 (for 2 marks).

The total value of the transfer was therefore £1,150,000 (£250,000 + £900,000). It was then
just a case of deducting the full nil rate band of £325,000, with lifetime tax calculated at the
rate of 20% (since the trust paid the inheritance tax arising).
This requirement was quite well answered, although a very common mistake was to exclude
the £50,000 held within cash ISAs from the cash element of £250,000. Even though the
requirement was to ignore the inheritance tax annual exemption, quite a few candidates still
deducted this. Despite the scenario clearly stating that the trust paid the inheritance tax
arising, a number of candidates grossed up the tax due using a rate of 20/80ths.
Requirement (c)
The gift impacted on Jessica’s savings income and her dividend income.
Savings income: If the gift had not been made, Jessica would have received savings income
of £6,250 on the cash held during the tax year, of which £1,250 would have been from ISAs.
Dividend income: If the gift had not been made, Jessica would have had dividend income of
£24,000. This was reduced to £8,000 as a result of making the gift of shares.
There were many perfect answers to this requirement, although answers were often more
complicated than they needed to be.
Savings income: The ISA intere st was not relevant (being exempt), so the income tax
reduction was simply £5,000 (£6,250 – £1,250) at 45% = £2,250 for 1.5 marks. Any attempt
to include the personal allowance made it impossible to score full marks.
Dividend income: Here, the income tax reduction was £16,000 (£24,000 – £8,000) at 39.35%
= £6,296 for 1.5 marks. The dividend nil rate band often caused unnecessary complications,
although full marks were still available if the nil rate band was deducted from both ‘before
gift’ and ‘after gift’ computations.
Candidates should be careful to use the correct tax rates which are clearly shown in the tax
tables available in the exam.

Flower Ltd is a trading company. Its results for the year ended 31 March 2026 include the

£

Accrued at 31 March 2026 5,000
Loan interest payable:
On loan to purchase a fleet of delivery vans (10,000)
On loan to buy shares in an unrelated trading company (8,000)

calculation of taxable total profits for the year ended 31 March 2026?

218 £32,000
Non-trade loan relationship income
£

Loan interest accrued 5,000
Interest payable on loan to buy shares (8,000)
–––––––
Taxable total profits 32,000

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

Loan interest receivable will always be non-trade loan relationship (NTLR) income unless the
company is in the trade of money lending. Th e interest received and accrued will both be
taxable, as the income is assessable on the accruals basis.
The non-trade loan interest payable will be deducted from the interest receivable when
calculating NTLR income. The loan to purchase the delivery vehicles is for trade purposes and
therefore it will be deducted from the trading profits (rather than go through NTLR). However,
the loan to buy shares in another company is an investment and is not for trading purposes
and so this amount will be deducted from interest receivable.

£

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

Property income for a company is always taxed on an accruals basis, therefore the payment
of electricity consumed during the accounting period but paid for after the end of the
accounting period is still included as an expense.
Interest payable in relation to an investment property (i.e. mortgage interest) is not
deductible from property income for companies. Instead, the interest payable is deductible
from interest income in calculating the non-trading loan relationship income as it relates to a
non-trading activity.
The treatment for individuals is different; interest payable on an investment property is not
deductible from property income and instead is deductible at the basic tax rate from the
income tax liability.

Q227 · Question 227
+10 XPA · MCQ
227 December 2020 OT question
Giant Ltd is a large company, and therefore pays its corporation tax by instalments.
For the eight-month period ended 31 August 2025, the company estimated that its
corporation tax liability would be £400,000.
What would Giant Ltd’s first corporation tax instalment be in respect of the eight-month
period ended 31 August 2025, and what is the due date of this instalment.

£

RELIEF FOR TRADING LOSSES
✅ Answer: D
💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

A large company is required to pay its final instalment of corporation tax by the 14th day of
the 4th month after the end of the accounting period (AP). Note that for a 12-month AP this
is 16 months after the start of the AP.
Where an AP is less than 12 months, the first instalment is due by the 14th day of the
7th month after the start of the AP. Subsequent instalments are due at 3 monthly intervals
thereafter, until the date of the final instalment is reached.
For an eight-month AP instalments are due on the 14th day of months 7, 10 and 12 (the last
being 4 months after the end of the AP). For this scenario, that is 14 July 2025, 14 October
2025 and 14 December 2025.
The first two instalments are calculated as 3/8 × corporation tax liability (£400,000 × 3/8 =
£150,000). The final instalment will be 2/8 × corporation tax liability.

📋 Examiner’s Report

A number of candidates selected B £100,000 on 14 July 2025, which is the correct due date
however the instalment amount (calculated as £400,000 × 3/12, giving £100,000) is incorrect
because £100,000 would be the amount payable if the period had been 12 months (rather
than eight months) long.
RELIEF FOR TRADING LOSSES

Q237 · Question 237

237 Computer Ltd owns 75% of Chair Ltd, 60% of Bin Ltd and 100% of Paper Inc. Paper Inc owns
75% of Cardboard Ltd. All companies are resident in the UK except Paper Inc, which is
resident in the US.

Chair Ltd
Bin Ltd

237
Loss can be surrendered to
Chair Ltd ✓
Bin Ltd 
Paper Inc
Cardboard Ltd ✓

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

A group relief loss group consists of a company and directly/indirectly owned companies
where there is a shareholding of at least 75%. Therefore, Bin Ltd is not in the loss group as
Computer Ltd’s direct shareholding is only 60%.
Computer Ltd has a direct holding of 75% in Chair Ltd and 100% in Paper Inc and an indirect
75% holding, through Paper Inc, in Cardboard Ltd (100% × 75%).
An overseas company can be part of the loss group structure but it cannot itself claim or
surrender losses, so losses cannot be surrendered to Paper Inc.

Q238 · Question 238

✅ Answer: C
💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

A capital gains group comprises the parent company and its 75% subsidiaries and also, the
75% subsidiaries of the first subsidiaries and so on.
The parent company must have an effective interest of over 50%, in ALL companies.
Acasta Ltd has a 75% interest in Barge Ltd and greater than 50% effective interest in
Dhow Ltd. Eight Ltd is not in the capital gains group as although it is an effective 51%
subsidiary of Acasta Ltd, it is not a direct 75% subsidiary of Coracle Ltd.

Q240 · Question 240

240 Battery Ltd owns 100% of Watch Ltd. During the six-month period ended 31 March 2026

✅ Answer: B
💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

profits and losses must be time apportioned, to find the relevant amounts falling within the
corresponding accounting period.
In this situation, the maximum loss that can be surrendered = lower of:
• Taxable total profits in the claimant company for the corresponding accounting period

• Allowable loss in the surrendering (loss-making) company for the corresponding
accounting period = £25,000 (3/12 × £100,000).

What is the total number of companies for the purposes of adjusting the upper and lower
limits for calculating the corporation tax of Telephone Ltd for the year ended 31 March
2026?
✅ Answer: C
💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

There are five associated companies (Telephone Ltd, Desk Ltd, Chair Ltd, Window Inc and
Blind Ltd) for the purposes of adjusting the upper and lower limits (for tax rate purposes) for
the year ended 31 March 2026.
Associated companies are those companies that are under the control of Telephone Ltd
(i.e. Telephone Ltd owns, either directly or indirectly, more than 50% of the company’s
ordinary share capital).
The upper and lower limits (for tax rate purposes) are adjusted for the number of associated
companies in the accounting period, regardless of when in that period they were acquired or
disposed. Therefore, Blind Ltd is included for the year ended 31 March 2026.
Overseas companies are included but dormant companies are excluded.

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

🔑 Key Answer Tips

This ten mark question concerns the adjustments to a company’s tax adjusted trading profit,
capital allowances computations and company payment dates.

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

The AIA (and where relevant) WDA must be adjusted to reflect the short accounting period of
six months.
The balance of the expenditure after AIA qualifies for the 50% FYA on the SRP. FYAs are never
time apportioned for a short period. WDAs will not be available on the remainder of the new
expenditure until the following period.


5
Instalment date

Where the accounting period is less than 12 months:
• First instalment due by: 14th day of 7th month after the start of the accounting period
(as normal).
• Subsequent instalments are due at three monthly intervals thereafter, until the date of
the final instalment (see below) is reached.
• Last instalment due by: 14th day of 4th month after the end of the accounting period.
Earlier instalments (as above) are only due if they fall before the date of the final
instalment.

🔑 Key Answer Tips

This section B question tests some common areas of corporation tax, including various
elements of administration, which can lead to easy marks if the rules are learnt. These
include augmented profits threshold for paying instalments, the amount of each instalment
and the due dates.
It also tests the additions that qualify as plant and machinery for capital allowance purposes
and the rules on calculating property business profits for a company.

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

The augmented profits include the dividends received because they were received from a non-
associated company (£770,000 + 45,000 = £815,000).
The instalment threshold is divided by three because Mixture Ltd has two associated
companies, so there are a total of three companies in the group (£1,500,000/3 = £500,000).

Mixture Ltd is paying corporation tax at 25% as the augmented profits exceed £250,000.
For a 12-month accounting period, instalments are due in four equal amounts. Although
Mixture may not have known how much the final corporation tax liability would be at the
time the first instalment was paid, the amount due is always one quarter of the total. If
instalments are under or over paid, then interest will be payable or receivable.
3

First instalment 14 October 2025
Last instalment 14 July 2026

Items which are included as part of the building (i.e. the staircase and walls) are not classed
as plant as they form part of the setting of the business.

Remember that property income is always taxed on an accruals basis for companies.
Therefore, it is important to consider the rent receivable and the expenses payable for the
accounting period.

🔑 Key Answer Tips

A fairly straightforward corporation tax loss question testing the different reliefs available. It
covers the factors affecting the choice of loss relief, carry forward of losses, current year and
prior year relief and terminal loss relief.
1
Relevant Not relevant
Timing of relief ✓
Extent to which losses will be wasted ✓
Extent to which QCD relief will be wasted ✓
Rate of corporation tax saved ✓ 

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

The timing of the relief obtained is relevant as a claim against total profits in the current year
and previous 12 months will result in earlier relief than a claim to carry a loss forward, and
such a claim will normally result in a tax repayment as well.
Losses may be lost on a cessation of trade if th ey have not previously been utilised, so this is
a relevant factor.
The extent to which relief for qualifying charitable donations will be lost is relevant, since
these cannot be carried forward.
The rate of corporation tax saved is not currently relevant as Loser Ltd is paying tax at 19%
through all periods as Loser Ltd’s profits never exceed £50,000.

It is possible to make a partial claim when offsetting trading losses brought forward from
earlier periods. Loser Ltd will therefore restrict the claim to avoid wasting QCDs. There is no
requirement to make a current period claim before carrying the loss forward.

The trading loss for the final 12 months of trading can be relieved against total profits for the
previous 36 months, on a LIFO basis, under the terminal loss relief rules.

🔑 Key Answer Tips

This corporation tax question involves a company with shareholdings in a number of other
companies. Provided the relevant group definitions had been learnt there were easy marks
available for identifying the associated companies and calculating the maximum group relief
claim.
The question also tests rollover relief, which is commonly tested in corporation tax questions
as it is the only relief against gains available to a company. Finally, it tests the rules for an
inter-group transfer of an asset for gains purposes.
1
Associated company
Eins Ltd ✓
Zwei Ltd
Drei Ltd ✓
Vier Co ✓

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

Two companies are associated companies if:
– One of the companies is under the control of the other, or
– Both are under the control of the same person or persons.
Control is where more than 50% of the ordinary share capital is directly or indirectly owned.
It does not matter where a company is resident so overseas companies are included in the
definition.

Your first step should be to identify which companies are in a group relief group with
Deutsch Ltd. You can then identify how much group relief is available.
• Deutsch Ltd cannot claim group relief from Eins Ltd as this company is not a 75%
subsidiary. However, Drei Ltd and Deutsch Ltd are in a group relief group.
• The maximum amount of group relief that can be claimed is £64,700 being
Drei Ltd’s trading loss of £52,700 plus the unrelieved qualifying charitable
donations of £12,000.

• The surrendering company may surrender any amount of its current period losses.
• There is no requirement for the surrendering company to relieve the loss against its
own profits first.
• The current period losses which may be surrendered are trading losses, unrelieved
QCDs and unrelieved property losses.

Where there is only partial reinvestment of the proceeds on disposal, the amount that has not
been reinvested is immediately chargeable to tax. The balance of the indexed gain can be
rolled over into the purchase of the new asset.

Berlin Ltd owns more than 75% of Zwei Ltd. The two companies therefore form a group for
capital gains purposes.
Assets transferred within a gains group are automatically transferred at no gain/no loss
(i.e. without a chargeable gain or allowable loss arising).
The transfer is deemed to take place at a price that does not give rise to a gain or a loss
(i.e. the indexed cost at the date of the transfer).
The transferor’s deemed proceeds figure is also the deemed cost of the acquiring company.

The claim for group relief must be made by Deutsch Ltd (the claimant company) on its
corporation tax return by 31 March 2028 (within two years of the end of the accounting period
when the loss is group relieved).
The claim for rollover relief must be made within four years of the end accounting period in
which the assets are sold and replaced (whichever is later) i.e. 31 March 2030 in this scenario.

Time limits for claims and elections should represent easy marks provided that you have learnt
them prior to the examination.

🔑 Key Answer Tips

This question is really three separate corporation tax questions.
Part (a) required the calculation of the corpor ation tax liability for a four-month period. As
you attempt this part of the question be careful with any areas that require time
apportionment, particularly capital allowances. Forgetting to time apportion can lose easy
marks in the exam.
Part (b)(i) looks at tax evasion versus tax avoidance. Ethics will always feature in the TX exam,
so you should ensure that you have prepared for the various scenarios that you could be
faced with. These are some of the easiest marks to achieve in the exam, so make sure you
allow time to attempt this part properly.
The final part of the question tests your higher skills, as it asks you to recalculate two of the
figures in the computation if the accounting period was 12 months long instead of four
months long. Think about what apportionments you made for the four-month period in part
(a) and calculate those figures again without the apportionment.

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

For companies, income and expenses associated with borrowing and lending money are dealt
with according to the loan relationship rules.
Where there is a trading loan relationship (as is the case here) the income receivable or
expense payable belongs in trading profits.
Where there is a non-trading loan relationship the income receivable or expense payable
belongs in non-trading loan relationships.
For companies the accruals basis will always be applied to the interest income or interest
expense.

This is the grant of a short (≤50 years) lease by the landlord to the tenant (Harbour Ltd). The
landlord will be taxed on a proportion of the lease premium in the year of receipt. Where the
tenant uses the lease in their trade they can claim an allowable deduction against their
trading profits on the accruals basis.
Alternative calculation for the deductible lease premium:
((51 – n)/50) × premium = amount taxed on landlord/number of years of lease = annual
deduction.
Where n= number of years of the lease to the nearest whole number of years.
(51 – 20)/50 × £78,000 = £48,360.

Tutorial notes
The AIA is time apportioned according to the length of the accounting period.
Long life assets are specifically allocated to the special rate pool. The balance of the
expenditure after the AIA is eligible for the 50% FYA, which is not time apportioned for the
short period. The balance after the 50% FYA is added to the special rate pool and will be
eligible for a 6% WDA in the following accounting period.
(b) (i) Tax evasion and tax avoidance
Tax evasion is illegal and involves the reduction of tax liabilities by not
providing information to which HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) is entitled,
or providing HMRC with deliberately false information.
In contrast, tax avoidance involves the minimisation of tax liabilities by the use
of any lawful means.
If Harbour Ltd extends its accounting period in order to save corporation tax,
then HMRC will not view this as tax evasion because it is quite lawful for the
company to prepare accounts up to whatever accounting date it wishes.

(ii) Capital allowances
Since the full amount of annual investment allowance will be available, capital
allowances will increase to £548,000 (£548,000 × 100%).
Chargeable gain
The capital loss will be offset against Harbour Ltd’s chargeable gain because
they will arise within the same acco unting period. This will reduce the
company’s chargeable gain to £62,300 (£104,300 – £42,000).


Tutorial notes
The accounting period will now be 12 months long, eliminating the need to time apportion
the AIA and therefore the full £1 million will be available to cover the expenditure on long life
assets (£548,000).
As the expenditure will now be covered by the AIA, there will be no 50% FYA.
Capital losses can only be offset against current period gains and then carried forwards
against future gains. It is not possible to carry back a capital loss. If the accounts are prepared
for the year ended 30 November 2026 both the capital gain and the capital loss will fall in the
same period, allowing the capital loss to offset the gain.

📋 Examiner’s Report

The corporation tax question should have been relatively straightforward, although some
basic tax planning is covered in part (b)(ii).
An important point to note is that Harbour Ltd is going to prepare accounts for a four-month
period. When reading through the question, candidates should therefore take a note that
this is going to impact on the calculation of the lease premium deduction, capital allowances
and property business income.
Then when candidates are planning the layout of their answer, it should be apparent that
separate workings are only required for the lease premium and capital allowances.
Everything else can be dealt with within the main computation, with just one column
required for the figures. Note how the workings for interest payable and for the property
business income are included in the model answer.


The main computation must commence with the computation of Harbour Ltd’s operating
profit, which is then followed by other inco me (property business income and chargeable
gain). The corporation tax figure follows after the main computation.
There are two very important points here:
Negative figures should be clearly shown by entering them as such on the spreadsheet. It is
very difficult for markers to pick up negative figures if all figures are shown positive, with the
total calculated within the cell on the lines of A1 + A2 – A3 + A4. It is also very easy to make
mistakes using this approach. If negative figures are entered, the total is simply SUM(A1:A4).
Requirement (a) – 10 marks
As the note states, answers should commence with the operating profit. Any different
approach makes an answer quite difficult to mark, especially an answer which attempts to
rewrite the statement of profit or loss.
Figures should not be combined. For example, the amortisation add back of £1,300 and the
lease premium deduction of £806 should not be shown as £494, especially as £494 was also
a fairly common incorrect answer for the lease premium deduction. It should also be noted
that since the lease premium consists of a payment, it simply cannot result in an income
entry.
There are a couple of aspects which require obvious care:
• Interest paid in the statement of profit or loss is £24,600. Accruals at the beginning
and end of the period are £20,500 and £12, 300 respectively. The correct figure (on a
payable basis) to deduct in working out the trading profit is therefore £24,600 –
£20,500 + £12,300 = £16,400.
• With the property business income, the rent has been received for six months, but the
insurance paid for 12 months. Given the four-month accounting period, the calculation
is therefore (£15,600 × 4/6) – (£1,800 × 4/12) = £9,800.
Question practice will eliminate mistakes such as giving an annual exempt amount (which is
not available for companies) against the chargeable gain, thereby losing a very easy ½ mark.
Also, candidates should appreciate that both the annual investment allowance and [first
year] allowance are given for the same asset if the annual investment allowance expenditure
limit is exceeded. In this case, the annual investment expenditure limit was reduced to
£1,000,000 × 4/12 = £333,333 because of the four-month accounting period.
Requirement (b)(i) – 3 marks
The fact that this requirement is just for 3 marks, together with the use of ‘briefly’ should be
a very good indication that only a short set of answers is required. This is why it is important
to make use of the model answers since candidates’ answers should not be any longer.
If tax evasion and tax avoidance are muddled up, the available marks are obviously going to
be lost, so candidates should think first, writ e second. The key point is that tax evasion is
illegal, whereas tax avoidance is legal.
As regards Harbour Ltd extending its accounting period, the company can do this provided
company law requirements are met (and these are not relevant to the tax examination).
Therefore, candidates cannot expect to get the full mark available if there [are] any caveats
to their answer. HM Revenue & Customs will not s ee this is as tax evasion, nor is there any
possibility of a compliance check being carried as a result of the change.

Requirement (b)(ii) – 2 marks
A quick read of the requirement should make it clear that it is not necessary to calculate any
tax saving or provide an explanation. The detail in the model answer is just there to help
candidates follow the workings.
With a 12-month accounting period, the full annual investment allowance of £1,000,000 is
available, so the annual investment allowance becomes £548,000.
The capital loss now arises within the same accounting period, so can be offset against
Harbour Ltd’s chargeable gain.
The 2 marks available again indicate the length of answer required.
Note: The examiner’s report has been edited in relation to comments on elements of the
question that have been amended due to changes in legislation and terminology.

1 May 2025 to 30 September 2025 (the period of account to 30 September 2025 being split
into two accounting periods), and a half mark for the period from 1 October 2025 (from the
date of the final financial statements) to 28 February 2026 (completion of winding up).
This requirement was generally well answered, although many candidates either did not
appreciate that there was an accounting period running from 1 October 2025 to 28 February
2026, or they had just the one period running from 1 May 2025 to 28 February 2026.
Requirement (b) – 9 marks
With this type of answer containing additions and deductions, candidates should be careful
to indicate which is which. A single column approach with deductions included as such on the
spreadsheet avoids any confusion. It is then just a matter of using the SUM function to get to
a figure for taxable total profits. Candidates who added up their total figure on a cell-by-cell
basis (e.g. A1 + A2 + A3 etc) invariably had problems when it came to negative entries, and it
was sometimes difficult for markers to determine whether a figure was a plus or a minus.
None of the adjustments or entries really needed separate workings. The capital allowances
were simply £220,000 at 100%, and £30,000 at 18% (for one mark in each case), and the gain
was calculated as the proceeds of £204,000 less the reinvestment of £168,000 (1.5 marks).
This requirement was generally very well answ ered. The only aspects which consistently
caused problems were the two interest figures and the chargeable gain. It was somewhat
surprising to see a number of candidates adding the figure for interest payable and deducting
the figure for interest receivable. Such carelessness cost a half mark in each case.
With the chargeable gain, it was clearly stated that Elara Ltd had made a claim to rollover the
gain, so this should have represented a fairly easy 1.5 marks.
Many candidates forgot to make the deduction for the qualifying charitable donations, even
where they had correctly added them back earlier in their computation.
Requirement (c) – 4 marks
There were quite a number of perfect answers to this requirement, although a number of
candidates did not appreciate that payment of a dividend and the advance rental payment
would not impact Fenrir Ltd’s corporation tax liability for year ending 31 March 2026. This is
because dividends are paid out of post-tax profits, and (given the accruals basis of accounts
preparation) rent paid in advance would not be deductible for the year ended 31 March 2026.
Having worked out the adjustments, candidates then needed to calculate the tax saving. This
could either be done by multiplying the adjustment by the corporation tax rate of 25%, or
working out a revised corporation tax liability and comparing this to the previous liability.
Well prepared candidates were able to answer this requirement quickly (a benefit of question
practice), scoring a fairly straightforward four marks and saving time. However, a correct
answer for the car – along with the 25% tax saving – was sufficient to score half of the marks.
🔑 Key Answer Tips

This question covers various aspects of corporation tax for three separate limited companies.
You need to determine accounting periods, calculate taxable total profits, and assess the tax
savings from specific measures. There is no overlap between the three requirements.
For Deimos Ltd, remember that an accounting period cannot exceed 12 months and consider
the impact that this will have on their accounting periods.
For Elara Ltd's taxable total profits, start with the given operating profit and systematically
adjust for non-allowable expenses and non-trading income. Make sure you are clear on which
items should be added back and which should be deducted. For capital allowances, identify
assets qualifying for the AIA and WDA and any FYAs, if relevant. The disposal of the
warehouse requires careful consideration of rollover relief.
For Fenrir Ltd, calculate the corporation tax savings from the proposed measures. Ensure you
calculate the tax impact of each measure at the appropriate corporation tax rate. Bear in
mind that not all the measures will necessarily save any tax.

Requirement (a) – 15 marks
Commencing with the operating profit, candidates were required to adjust for the following:

non-allowable. The majority of candidates correctly adjusted for four or five of the items,
although the amortisation and/or the qualif ying charitable donations were sometimes
missed. For this style of question, it is very important that candidates clearly indicate whether
items are being added or deducted. A single column layout is therefore recommended.
Leasehold premium (3 marks): Many candidates had no difficulty calculating the correct
deduction for the grant of a 12-year lease. One common mistake, however, was to work out
the non-chargeable portion of the lease (£96,000 × 2% × (12 – 1) = £21,120) and then use
that for the basis of the lease deduction rather than working out the chargeable portion
(£96,000 – £21,120 = £74,880). Although most candidates appreciated that the chargeable
portion then had to be divided by the number of years of the lease (12 years), quite a few did
not then apply the 6/12ths restriction; the lease being granted on 1 October 2025.
An alternative approach to calculating the chargeable portion of the lease was £96,000 × (51
– 12)/50 = £74,880. If using this approach, candidates needed to take care as the incorrect
number of years (51 years and 12 years) were often used.
It was also important to realise that the final result had to be deducted in the main
computation.
Regardless of approach, it is not recommended to attempt the entire working within the one
spreadsheet cell. For example, missing the brackets on £96,000 × 51 – 12/50 would give an
answer of £4,896,000. Provided the correct wo rkings are shown, appropriate marks will be
awarded even if a candidate makes an arithmetical error. Without workings, it can be difficult
determining what the candidate’s intention is.
Capital allowances (5.5 marks): There were quite a lot of marks for a capital allowances
computation, so care was needed. It was pleasing to see many perfect answers, but some
candidates struggled here. It was necessary to decide whether an asset purchase qualified
for the 100% annual investment allowance, and, if not qualifying , whether the purchase went
into the main pool or the special rate pool.
The aspect which caused most difficulty was the disposal of the car purchased during the
same year. The correct treatment was to add the addition and to deduct the disposal
proceeds from the special rate pool. However, many candidates kept this car separate and
calculated a balancing adjustment.
Other income (2 marks): The other income consisted of bank interest (it was necessary to
add in a year end accrual), dividends from an 80% UK subsidiary company (this was exempt
income) and a chargeable gain (the profit before taking account of the indexation allowance
was also given).
Once again, there were a lot of perfect answers here. Typical mistakes included deducting
the bank interest accrual, treating the dividend as taxable, and using the pre-indexed gain or
deducting the annual exempt amount of £3,000. This is why question practice is so important
because these are the type of mistakes which if made once, are less likely to be repeated.

Deductions (1.5 marks): After adding it back to trading profits earlier, the qualifying
charitable donation now had to be deducted from total profits for a half mark. A group relief
deduction was also available in respect of a trading loss made by the 80% UK subsidiary
company. There was one mark for this, but only a half mark if not deducted at the correct
point in the main computation or if the loss was restricted to 80%.
Corporation tax (0.5 mark): The final mark was for calculating the corporation tax liability.
This generally wasn’t a problem, although a few candidates kept the chargeable gain separate
and then applied a different rate of tax on this. [Note that when this question was originally
set there was only one rate of corporation tax and this calculation was for only half a mark.]
As already mentioned, with computations containing both additions and deductions,
candidates should be very careful to indicate which is which. A single column approach with
deductions included as such on the spreadsheet avoids any confusion. It is then just a matter
of using the SUM function to get to a figure fo r taxable total profits. The simplicity of this
approach is that the same layout can be used regardless of whether a profit or a loss is
involved.
The only aspects of the answer which warranted separate workings were the leasehold
premium and the capital allowances. Everything else was easily dealt with within the main
computation.
Layout is not something candidates should really be concerned about on the day. With
sufficient question practice, the correct layout becomes automatic.
Note: The examiner’s report has been edited to remove comments on elements of the
question that have been amended due to changes in legislation.

The building costs are not plant and machinery so do not qualify for regular capital
allowances. However, they will qualify for structures and buildings allowance (see below).
The integral features are allocated the AIA first as they would otherwise be added to the
special rate pool. The remaining assets also qualify for the AIA as the total additions are less
than £1,000,000 and there has been no AIA used already. The AIA should be claimed in
preference to full expensing as then there will not be a potential balancing charge on disposal.
(W3) Structures and buildings allowance
£93,300 × 3% × 4/12 = £933

In the TX exam, structures and buildings allowance (SBA) can be claimed on renovations or
extensions made to existing buildings on or after 1 April 2020. They are claimed from the date
the building is available for use, therefore, the building costs of the extension are eligible for
SBA from 1 December 2025. The other items are plant and machinery, and do not qualify for
SBA. SBA should always be kept separate to capital allowances on plant and machinery.

📋 Examiner’s Report

Corporation tax computation
Again, many workings for this style of question can be included within the main computation.
The order of items within the main computatio n should generally follow the layout of the
question. This is especially the case if a question is based around a partly completed draft
corporation tax computation which includes some correct figures.
Candidates should be aware that when it comes to capital allowances in relation to a newly
constructed building, the construction cost of the building itself does not qualify for plant
and machinery capital allowances.
[Sections of this examiner’s report have been deleted because they relate to parts of the
question which have been amended.]
As regards property business income, candidates should be aware that the cost of initial
repairs will be disallowable capital expenditure if the property could not have been let out in
its original state and this was reflected in the purchase price paid.
Where figures for chargeable gains are given, then these figures should not be recalculated.
The only reason for giving more information (proceeds and expenditure) is so that the
indexation allowance can be calculated.
Where there are two or more gains, then each gain should be dealt with separately. When it
comes to the indexation allowance, note that:
• There is no indexation allowance for any expenditure incurred after December 2017.
• The indexation allowance cannot create a capital loss.

260 E-COMMERCE PLC (ADAPTED) Walk in the footsteps of a top tutor

1 The issue of preference shares is not a trading expense and therefore the associated
legal fees are not an allowable deduction.
2 Legal fees are treated in the same way as the loan they relate to. The loan was for
trading purposes, therefore the fees are a deductible trading expense.
3 Legal fees relating to a lease are only deductible if it is the renewal of a short (50 years
or less) lease. The lease here is over 50 years long and as such the legal fees are not an
allowable deduction for tax purposes and need to be added back.
4 Legal fees in relation to the registration of trademarks relate to the trade, and are
therefore tax deductible.
5 Since it is only the life of the lease which wa s incorrect in the original calculation, this
can be corrected by simply multiplying the figure given by the 12 years used originally
and dividing by the correct figure of 15 years. It is not necessary to try to recalculate
the deduction from scratch, and this would prove very difficult as the figure for the
premium paid was not provided in the question.
6 Cars 1 and 2 have CO₂ emissions between 1 and 50 grams per kilometre, and qualify
for writing down allowances at the rate of 18%. No adjustment is therefore required.
7 Car 3 has CO₂ emissions over 50 grams per kilometre, and therefore only qualifies for
writing down allowances at the rate of 6%. The extra 12% (18% – 6%) that had been
calculated originally therefore needs to be deducted from the total capital allowances.
8 Car 4 has zero emissions, and therefore qualifies for 100% first year allowance. In the
absence of any other information, assume that cars purchased are new (not second-
hand). Therefore, an additional allowance of 82% (100% – 18%) needs to be included.
9 The scrapping of the computer equipment is a disposal for capital allowances purposes.
The company should therefore have received a 100% balancing allowance rather than
a writing down allowance at the rate of 18%. The 82/18 adjustment represents the
additional 82% (100% – 18%) of the brought forward TWDV which can be deducted.
This could also have been calculated by comparing the correct balancing allowance
(£1,512/18% = £8,400) with the amount that had previously been deducted (£1,512).
10 As the repairs were carried out in order to make the warehouse usable, they are treated
as capital in nature and are therefore disallowed. However, structures and buildings
allowance (SBA) at 3% can be claimed on these costs since they were incurred after
1 April 2020 (the relevant date for TX exams). SBA can only be claimed from the date
the property was brought into use, i.e. the day it was first let out – 1 July 2025.
11 Property and interest income must be dealt with on an accruals basis, therefore an
adjustment is required for the rent due and the correct loan interest accrual.

(b) Quarterly instalment payments
🔑 Key Answer Tips

Part (a) involves correcting an existing tax computation, rather than preparing the
computation from scratch. This is a somewhat unusual presentation, although it is not
dissimilar to that seen in a couple of other corporation tax questions. Here, however, the
question is made slightly more difficult as it also involves reversing calculations which have
already been done (incorrectly) to calculate correct figures. This question was not popular
with students, many of whom did not know how to tackle it. It is important however, to
attempt every question in the examination and therefore you should set out the
computation, including the figures you do know, attempt the workings for those you don’t
(making assumptions if necessary), and then go on to calculate the corporation tax liability,
for which you will get follow through marks, even if parts of your answer are wrong. This part
is also for 12 marks, and you must make sure you don’t overrun on time here.
Part (b) requires you to identify why the company would not pay instalments in the current
year and why they would be due in the following year. This should be straightforward
provided these aspects of administration have been learnt.
The highlighted words in the answer are key phrases that markers are looking for.


(a) Revised corporation tax computation – year ended 31 March 2026

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

In a challenging question such as this, it is important to maximise marks with a systematic
approach, making sure you score all the easy marks (of which there are many). Start by laying
out your computation – inserting any obvious figures (e.g. figures provided in the question
which you know are correct) and leaving blank the more difficult ones. Then work through the
gaps, doing straightforward workings on the face of the computation and more detailed ones
in referenced workings underneath. If you are not sure, make a decision and move on, do not
waste time on one small point.
For some figures, you need to reverse calculations which have been carried out incorrectly
(some are not shown in the question), before doing revised calculations. This requires a good
understanding of the way the calculations work, rather than just the ability to follow the pro
forma and crunch the numbers. There are several ways these calculations could be presented.

Whilst it would be possible to calculate the capital allowances by doing a revised
computation, not all of the figures for that computation (such as the brought forward balance
on the main pool) were provided in the question. Therefore, it would be necessary to do
significantly more workings (to establish the missing figures) if this approach were taken. It is
therefore easier to simply correct the mistakes you are aware of via short workings as shown.



Being able to determine when corporation tax is payable is a common examination
requirement, and it is important to learn the rules about which companies must pay by
quarterly instalments and the exceptions from that system, which are relevant here.
• Large companies have to make quarterly instalment payments in respect of their
corporation tax liability. A large comp any is one with augmented profits
exceeding £1,500,000, adjusted for sh ort accounting periods and associated
companies.
• However, a company is not required to make quarterly instalment payments in
the first year that it is large.
Therefore, E-Commerce plc will not have been required to make instalment
payments for the year ended 31 March 2026 as it was not a large company in
the year ended 31 March 2025.
This is because the augmented profits of £1,360,000 were less than £1,500,000.
• For the year ended 31 March 2027, this exception will not apply. Therefore,
E-Commerce plc will have to make quarterly instalment payments as its
augmented profits will exceed £1,500,000.

📋 Examiner’s Report

Part (a) was not particularly difficult, but the information was presented in a different format
to previous questions of this nature. However, candidates would have benefited from
knowing the pro forma layout.
The requirement was generally reasonably we ll answered and there were a few highly
satisfactory answers. The deduction for the lease premium caused the most problems, with
many candidates not appreciating that there was no need to recalculate the amount taxed
on the landlord – thereby spending quite a bit of time unnecessarily.
Part (b) was also reasonably well answered, although to score full marks it was necessary for
answers to be quite precise – not, for example, just mentioning large companies, without
explaining what a large company is.

STRETCHED LTD (ADAPTED)
This scenario relates to two requirements.
Stretched Ltd has always prepared its accounts to 31 December, but has decided to change
its accounting reference date to 31 March. The company’s results for the 15-month period
ended 31 March 2026 are as follows:
1 The tax adjusted trading profit is £642,500. This figure is before taking account of

2 Until January 2026 the company has never been entitled to capital allowances as all
assets were leased. On 15 January 2026 the company bought office equipment for

(b) Advantages of 31 March year end
• Being aligned with the financial year will make it easier for a company to
calculate its corporation tax liability, since the same rates, reliefs and legislation
will apply throughout the accounting period.
• For owner-managed companies, alignment with the income tax year (the odd
five days can be ignored) will make it easier as regards calculating the most tax
efficient method of extracting profits from the company.

🔑 Key Answer Tips

This question requires the calculation of a company's taxable total profits for a three-month
accounting period. It encompasses adjustments to trading profit, capital allowances, and the
computation of a chargeable gain.
You should begin by adjusting the given accounting loss for non-allowable expenses. Make
sure you include a zero for the items where no adjustment is required as per the instructions
in the question. When calculating capital allowances remember to think about the impact of
the short accounting period on the different allowances.
When calculating the chargeable gain on the investment property, ensure you include all
incidental costs of acquisition and disposal. Apply indexation allowance to both the original
cost and any enhancement expenditure up to December 2017.
Finally, the trading loss should be offset against the total profits, and remember to deduct
any qualifying charitable donations.
