Tutorial notes

📋 Examiner’s Report

The corporation tax question was very well answered, with many candidates scoring high
marks. The question required candidates to calculate Cop Ltd’s trading loss and taxable total
profits for the three-month period 1 October to 31 December.
As for the income tax question, there were various ways of approaching this question. Again,
the easiest one was to have a main computation working out the trading loss, with this then
extended to include the chargeable gain and qualifying charitable donation to arrive at a
figure for taxable total profits. Capital allowances and the chargeable gain both warranted
separate workings.
In regard to the main computation, there were two issues which sometimes caused
problems:
• Candidates were instructed to indicate by the use of zero (0) any items which did not
require adjustment. There were in fact five items of expenditure where no adjustment
was required (because they were allowable), representing a total of 2.5 marks. A
number of candidates did not do as instructed and therefore would not have gained
these very easy 2.5 marks even if the remainder of their workings were correct.
Remember it is important to read and follow the instructions given in the requirement.
• With this type of answer containing both additions and deductions, candidates should
be very careful to indicate which is which. A single column approach with deductions
shown clearly as such on the spreadsheet avoids any confusion. Those candidates who
did not show the deductions clearly invariably had problems when it came to showing
totals with negative entries, and it was sometimes difficult for markers to determine
whether a figure was a plus or a minus.
One other point to bear in mind is that candidates should answer a question in the order in
which information is provided. The information was provided in the order (1) donations, (2)
legal and professional fees, (3) promotional costs and (4) annual party. So, adjustments
should follow the same sequence. If this a pproach is followed, it allows markers the
opportunity to sometimes award a mark where an obvious mistake has been made.
Capital allowances
The fact that the accounting period was only three months long meant care had to be taken
with the capital allowances working:
• The £1,000,000 annual investment allowance expenditure limit was £1,000,000 × 3/12
= £250,000.
• There was no restriction in regard to first-year allowances.
• The 18% and 6% writing down allowances were both restricted by 3/12ths.
Despite these complications, quite a number of candidates correctly calculated the capital
allowances figure for 5 marks, with many achieving 4 or 4.5 marks.
The main problem was with the car in the specia l rate pool which was bought (for £57,000)
and sold (for £50,000) during the accounting period. Despite this being the only asset in the
special rate pool, there was not a balancing adjustment, but, instead, a writing down
allowance calculated as normal.

Chargeable gain
The chargeable gain was probably the most difficult aspect of this question, especially as two
separate indexation allowance workings were necessary.
• The incidental costs had to be picked up from the disallowance of legal and
professional fees. This figure was then deducted from the disposal proceeds, so was
not relevant when it came to the indexation allowance calculations.
• One surprising mistake was sometimes the indexation allowances were calculated, but
then only those figures deducted and not the cost and enhancement expenditure
figures on which the indexation allowances were based.
Candidates should particularly note that the annual exempt amount is NOT relevant to
corporation tax.

📋 Examiner’s Report

For part (a), candidates were required to st ate whether the company was resident or not
resident in the UK for corporation tax purposes. This requirement resulted in a very surprising
amount of incorrect answers, with at least half the candidates deciding that the company
was not resident because of its central management and control being exercised overseas.
Part (b) required a calculation of the company’s trading loss, property business loss and
capital loss. As regards the trading loss, this involved pre-trading expenditure, a deduction
for a lease premium and capital allowances. This section was generally very well answered,
although there were a couple of consistent problems. Firstly, it was often not appreciated
that a second-hand car does not qualify for th e 100% first year allowance. [Part of the
examiner’s report has been removed as it relates to a topic which is no longer examinable.]
For part (c), candidates were required to explain how the company would have been able to
relieve its trading loss, property business loss and capital loss. Provided candidates
appreciated that it was the company’s first period of trading, this section was then well
answered. However, candidates who overlooked this basic fact spent a lot of time discussing
all the various (irrelevant) loss reliefs, with a few candidates discussing the income tax relief
for a loss incurred in the early years of a trade.

31 March 2025.
Requirement (a) – 7 marks
This requirement was not answered as well as may be expected, given it was a fairly
straightforward loss adjustment scenario:
• Several candidates failed to score very easy marks by not indicating the non-adjustable
items with a zero, despite being instructed to do so. There were seven such items, so
this basic mistake could have cost a potential 3.5 marks.
• The deduction for interest payable was ignored by many candidates, despite the
requirement specifically referring to this note in the question scenario. On the other
hand, few of those candidates who did include an adjustment computed the correct
figure. The interest figure included in the summarised income statement was £8,750.
This figure related to the period 1 Marc h to 30 September 2025. A further three
months of interest therefore had to be added (£5,000 × 3/6 = £2,500), making a total
interest deduction of £8,750 + £2,500 = £11,250.
• Some candidates attempted to rewrite the summarised statement of profit or loss in
order to get to the tax adjusted trading loss. Apart from ignoring the instruction to
commence with the operating loss figure, this approach was much more complicated;
making it difficult to gain all the marks.
• The requirement specifically instructed candidates to ignore the information given in
respect of the property business income and the chargeable gain, yet several
candidates did not comply with this and wasted quite a bit of their time.
• The best approach to this requirement was a single-column list commencing with the
operating loss as a negative figure and listing the items referred to in the relevant
notes. Provided the interest was also included as a negative, it was then just a case of
using the SUM function to get to the tax adjusted trading loss. The simplicity of this
approach is that the same layout can be used regardless of whether a profit or a loss
is involved.

Requirement (b) – 4 marks
There were many good answers for this requirement, with quite a few candidates achieving
full marks.
Candidates had to take account of the property business income, the chargeable gain and
the qualifying charitable donation, and were instructed in the requirement to only take
account of this information. However, a number of candidates included the trading loss or
even the taxable total profits for the previous period. Again, in doing so they would have
certainly wasted time.
The most common problem was with the chargeable gain where figures were provided for
both the original cost and for the indexed cost. Some candidates invariably deducted both
figures, and this resulted in a capital loss rath er than a chargeable ga in. Once again, this
shows why it is important to read the question and requirements as carefully as possible.
Requirement (c)(i) – 1 mark
The correct answer was by 31 December 2027, which is two years from the end of the loss-
making period.
There were few correct answers for this requi rement, with answers spread across a wide
range of alternative dates.
Requirement (c)(ii) – 3 marks
Although there were some perfect answers to this requirement, overall, it was not
particularly well answered.
Many candidates ignored the current period loss relief claim, with others calculating the
revised corporation tax liability for the ye ar ended 31 March 2025 rather than the
corporation tax refund.
The answer was simply the trading loss (calcula ted in part (a)), less the current year total
profits (the property business profits and chargeable gain from part (b)) at 25%. Even if this
approach was used, however, many candidates included the current year qualifying
charitable donation, thereby missing out on a half mark.
Quite a few candidates just stated that the co rporation tax originally paid would be fully
refunded. Although a mark was given for this, candidates needed to go further to gain any
additional marks. For example, if a candidate’s own-figure trading loss was greater than total
profits in the year ended 31 March 2025 (so that a full refund was in fact the correct answer),
a further half mark was given for an appropriate explanation.

📋 Examiner’s Report

The corporation tax question was generally quite well answered, although (somewhat
surprisingly) the capital allowances working in part (b) caused problems. Candidates often
ended up with a reasonably correct answer to part (c)(i), where loss relief was claimed, but
spent a lot of time on irrelevant workings in reaching that point.
One common problem seen in part (b) was the inability to deal with negatives. The
requirement was to calculate Mooncake Ltd's tax adjusted trading loss, commencing with
the operating loss figure of £93,820. This meant that the adjustments for non-allowable
expenditure reduced the amount of loss, but the loss was increased by capital allowances.
As shown in the suggested solution, the easies t approach was to start with £93,820 as a
negative figure, show non-allowable expenditure as positive figures and then include capital
allowances as another negative. This is then consistent with a profit adjustment question
commencing with a profit, avoiding the loss of some easy marks if negatives and positives
are confused. The total can then be obtained using the SUM function on the spreadsheet.
Some candidates showed all figures as positive and then tried to calculate the total within
the cell on the lines of – A1+A2+A3-A4. It is also very easy to make mistakes using this
approach.
The only aspect requiring a separate working was one for capital allowances.
Requirement (a)
Although many candidates easily picked up the [three] available marks, many instead wrote
at length about available loss reliefs.
The fact that this requirement is just for [3] marks, together with the use of ‘state’ should be
a very good indication that only a short set of answers is required. This is why it is important
to make use of the model answers since candidates’ answers should, ideally, not be any
longer than those.
Candidates who mentioned loss of personal allowances or annual exempt amounts had,
worryingly, confused income and corporation taxes.
Requirement (b)
When answering this type of question, candidates are advised to answer in the same order
as information is presented. So here, the first item was depreciation, and that, therefore,
should have been the first adjustment. This approach makes it easier for markers to follow a
candidate’s answer, and there is less scope for missing out any of the adjustments.
As can be seen from the suggested solution, the capital allowances working was fairly
straightforward, involving just a main pool. There were three disposal figures to deduct from
the brought forward written down value, with an 18% writing down allowance calculated on
the remaining balance. The only reason for pr oviding the cost figures was so that (where
relevant) proceeds could be restricted to original cost. However, many candidates included
the cost figures as additions, and there were then various permutations involving balancing
adjustments. Again, this is why question practice is so important.
It should also be noted that none of the other information (property business loss and profit
on disposal of shares) was relevant to this part of the question since the requirement was
just to calculate the tax adjusted trading loss.

Requirement (c)(i)
With only losses for the year ended 31 March 2026, there was obviously no income. However,
this should have been indicated by the use of zeros (0). There was no chargeable gain because
the indexation allowance of £6,700 exceeded the gain of £3,700. This did not create a loss,
and there was no need to utilise the capital loss brought forward from the year ended

266 MUSIC PLC (ADAPTED)
🔑 Key Answer Tips

In this question there are ten marks for written explanations of the gains group and
associated company rules. It is important to st ate the basic rule and then apply to the facts
of the question. Be careful with the overseas company, which is included but unable to enjoy
the benefits of gains group status.
The highlighted words in the answer are key phrases that markers are looking for.


(a) Capital gains group
• Companies form a capital gains group if at each level in the group structure there
is a 75% shareholding, provided the parent company has an effective interest of
more than 50%.
• Alto Ltd, Bass Ltd, Cello Ltd, Echo Inc and Flute Ltd are all 75% subsidiaries, and
Music plc has an effective interest of 60% (80% × 75%) in Flute Ltd. All of these
companies therefore form a capital gains group.
• However, Bass Ltd and Cello Ltd will only be included in respect of assets
acquired or disposed of whilst they were members of the group.
• Drum Ltd and Gong Ltd are not included as Drum Ltd is not a 75% subsidiary,
and Music plc’s effective interest in Gong Ltd is only 48% (80% × 75% × 80%).
• Although Echo Inc is included in the definition of the capital gains group,
companies that are resident overseas are not able to take advantage of the
provisions applicable to a capital gains group.
(b) Associated companies
• Alto Ltd, Bass Ltd, Cello Ltd, Echo In c, Flute Ltd and Gong Ltd are all under the
common control of Music plc, and are therefore associated companies.
• Companies associated for part of the accounting period, such as Bass Ltd and
Cello Ltd, count as associated companies for the whole of the period.
• For these purposes, it does not matter where a company is resident. Echo Inc is
therefore included despite being resident overseas.
• Drum Ltd is not included as an associated company since Music plc’s effective
interest in this company is only 45%.
(c) Corporation tax liability – year ended 31 March 2026

and b/f) may be set against this gain.

There are seven associated companies in the group including Music plc itself.
(d) Bank loan
Under the loan relationship rules, the cost of loans used for non-trade purposes are
deductible from interest income. If the loan was used to acquire a property which was
to be rented out (i.e. a non-trade purpose), the interest would not be deducted from
trading income, nor property business income (as for individuals), but from the
company’s interest income.
Legal fees
Legal fees incurred in relation to the purchase of a capital asset are not deductible
from the company’s trading profits. They will be deductible in the chargeable gain
computation when the building is ultimately sold.
Rent receivable
The rent receivable from letting the property to a tenant will be included on an accruals
basis, net of any allowable deductions, in taxable total profits as property income.

1 December 2023 (incorporation) to 31 March 2026 (the end of the first twelve-month set of
accounts, Ash Ltd having previously prepared accounts for the 14-month period ended
31 March 2025). This section was quite well answered.
If asked to identify a company’s accounting periods throughout a given period candidates
should make sure that all relevant periods are stated. It does not create a good impression if
there are gaps between the accounting periods stated by a candidate, or if a stated period
ends before it has started.
Part (a)(ii) required candidates to explain Ash Ltd’s residence status throughout the same
period. Candidates should be careful not to confuse the rules for companies with those
applicable to individuals. If a limited company is incorporated in the UK, then nothing else is
relevant. So, as regards the majority of Ash Ltd’s director/shareholders moving overseas,
candidates should just have stated that this did not have any impact on the company’s
residence status.
For Beech Ltd, a summarised statement of profit or loss was provided for the year ended
31 January 2026. The requirement for 6 marks was to calculate the company’s corporation
tax liability for this year. Various adjustment s were required, but there were no capital
allowances. This section was very well answered.
When making adjustments to a trading profit, candidates need to be very careful that
adjustments are correctly added and not deducted.
Cedar Ltd had made a chargeable gain on the disposal of a shareholding on 28 December
2025. For the year ended 31 March 2026, the company made a trading loss. Cedar Ltd was a
100% subsidiary company of Timber Ltd, and for the year ended 31 March 2026, Timber Ltd
had made a trading loss and also a capital loss.
Part (c) for 5 marks required a calculation of Cedar Ltd’s taxable total profits for the year
ended 31 March 2026. This was on the basis th at all available claims and elections were
made. This section was again well answered. When calculating chargeable gains for a
corporate share disposal carefully check the dates that have been given. There was a rights
issue which had taken place in the month of purchase, so there was no need to index prior
to adding the new shares into the share pool.

📋 Examiner’s Report

The corporation tax question was fairly well answered, although many candidates had
difficulty when it came to requirement (b).
Along with a trading profit, for the year ended 31 March 2026 Maximum Ltd had property
business income and chargeable gains. The company made qualifying charitable donations
and political donations during the year. Maximum Ltd had brought forward amounts of
trading loss, property business loss and capital loss.
Maximum Ltd had two subsidiary companies. Xim Ltd was a 75% group company, whereas
Mum Ltd (with a 65% shareholding) was not.
Requirement (a)
One important point to appreciate is that property business income and chargeable gains are
both included within the calculation of taxable total profits (TTP), yet a number of candidates
kept these elements entirely separate from the trading profit (even though all income and
gains form part of the TTP).
The starting point was to adjust the trading profit for three items:
Leasehold premium deduction (1.5 marks): The essential point to appreciate here was that
the figure provided was the amount of premium assessed on the landlord (£22,320), and not
the amount of premium itself. Therefore, the first step in the calculation had already been
done. The relevant deduction was simply the assessed amount divided by the number of years
of the lease (8 years), with an 8/12ths restriction; the lease being granted on 1 August 2025.
It was also important to realise that the final result (22,320/8 × 8/12 = £1,860) had to be
deducted in the main computation, not added.
Leasing costs disallowance (1.5 marks): Leasing costs for two cars had been deducted in
arriving at the trading profit. The first car had CO₂ emissions of 40 grams per kilometre, so no
adjustment was required. The second car had CO₂ emissions in excess of 50 grams per
kilometre, so a 15% add-back was required. This adjustment often caused problems, with
various mistakes made. For example, sometimes the 15% add-back was applied for both cars,
or adjustment was made for the 85% deductible element of the leasing costs for the second
car.
Deduction for employee bonuses (1 mark): Bonuses of £20,000 were paid on 30 November
2026, with a further £16,000 paid on 15 February 2027. No entitlement to the bonuses arose
until the time that they were paid. The essential point here is that only the bonuses paid
within nine months of the end of maximum Ltd’s period of account are deductible, so not
those paid on 15 February 2027.
Having calculated a revised trading profit figure, the next steps were to calculate the property
business income and chargeable gains:
Property business income (3 marks): This was a fairly straightforward computation for
3 marks based around a freehold warehouse which was let for a seven-month period before
the warehouse was subsequently sold. There were many perfect answers. Some candidates
struggled with the insurance payment, often trying to restrict this to the period the
warehouse was let out or owned by Maximum Ltd. However, it should have been obvious
that this aspect was taken into account due to Maximum Ltd receiving a refund of the
insurance premium paid. The correct deduction was therefore simply the insurance premium
paid (£1,320) less the refund (£190).

Chargeable gains (3 marks): The chargeable gains computation was somewhat more
complicated, although there were still a number of perfect answers. Some candidates did not
appreciate that they had been given the two relevant chargeable gain figures (a freehold
factory was sold as well as the freehold warehouse), so no chargeable gain calculations were
required. However, the gain on the disposal of the factory could be rolled over (the proceeds
being fully reinvested – and that is why proc eed figures were provided). The gain on the
disposal of the warehouse could not be rolled over because this property was not used for
business purposes. It was also necessary to deduct the brought forward capital loss as this
was automatically relieved (however, the mark available was given even if this deduction was
made in the answer to requirement (b)).
Donations (1 mark): Finally, it was a matter of deducting the qualifying charitable donations,
and indicating (by the use of a zero) that no deduction was available for the political
donations; many candidates missed an easy half mark by not showing this zero, despite being
instructed to do so.
As already mentioned, with computations containing both additions and deductions,
candidates should be very careful to indicate which is which. A single column approach with
deductions shown clearly as such on the spreadsheet avoids any confusion.
It is best to avoid putting workings for two or three marks within the one cell, which is what
some candidates did with their business property income calculation. It is very easy to make
mistakes, and workings have to be clearly shown in order for marks to be awarded.
Requirement (b)
This requirement caused a lot of problems. Even if answering correctly, candidates often took
a very long-winded approach towards a final answer, wasting considerable time in the
process. Also, with what were often a half page of notes and workings, it was sometimes
difficult to find a candidate’s final answer.
As already mentioned, Maximum Ltd had brought forward amounts of trading loss
(£288,200) and property business loss (£3,800). The brought forward capital loss should have
been set against the chargeable gain, and is therefore irrelevant to this requirement.
Simply taking the brought forward trading loss and using this against the (candidate’s own
figure) taxable total profits of Maximum Ltd for the year ended 31 March 2026 scored
1.5 marks. Add in the brought forward property business loss, and that scored half the
available marks.
The other two marks were for dealing with the group relief aspects. One problem here,
however, was that some candidates got into considerable confusion by treating the trading
profits of the two subsidiary companies instead as trading losses. The correct treatment was
to offset the brought forward trading loss against the trading profit of Xim Ltd (£21,400), and
then to show or state that no relief was av ailable against the profits of Mum Ltd. Many
candidates – despite correctly dealing with Xim Ltd – did not mention Mum Ltd.
Rather than an extensive set of workings, th e entire 4-mark answer was therefore simply
£288,200 + £3,800 – own figure taxable total profits – £21,400 – £0.

Registration, output & input tax, special schemes, partial exemption, administration

Q271 · Question 271
+10 XPA · MCQ
271 March/June 2024 OT question
Which TWO of the following taxpayers are most likely to benefit financially from voluntary
registration for value added tax (VAT)?
of the public
of the public
the public
VAT-registered businesses
⚡ Select ALL correct options (A, D)
✅ Answer: A and D
271 A and D
Voluntary registration is beneficial for traders who can recover their input VAT and either
make zero rated supplies (so will not have to charge higher prices inclusive of VAT), or make
supplies to other VAT registered businesses (who can recover the additional cost of the
output VAT charged).
A business which buys zero rated supplies and sells standard rated goods to members of the
public, will not benefit by voluntary registration since it will not recover VAT on its purchases
(as these have no VAT being zero rated) and will have to charge members of the public an
extra 20% to recover the VAT on sales.
A business which buys zero rated supplies and sells zero rated goods to members of the
public will not benefit from voluntary registration as there is no VAT to be charged on sales
or recovered on expenses.
Q272 · Question 272
+10 XPA · MCQ
272 March/June 2022 OT question
Frances started trading on 1 January 2025. An analysis of her taxable supplies for the first
year of trading (spread evenly over the quarter) is as follows:
Quarter ended £
31 March 2025 16,000
30 June 2025 21,000
30 September 2025 31,000
31 December 2025 34,000
Frances notifies HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) of her liability to compulsorily register for
value added tax (VAT) on time.
From what date will Frances be registered for VAT?
✅ Answer: B
272 B
Frances’ taxable turnover exceeds £90,000 on 30 November 2025 (16,000 + 21,000 + 31,000
+ 2/3 × 34,000) = £90,667. She has 30 days to notify HM Revenue & Customs and is registered
from the 1st day of the month following the registration deadline, i.e. 1 January 2026.
📋 Examiner’s Report

The other incorrect options are:
A 30 December 2025 being 30 days after historic test exceeded
C 31 January 2026 being one month after quarter end when historic test exceeded
D 1 February 2026 which would be correct if the historic test was met on 31 December
2025

Q273 · Question 273
+10 XPA · MCQ
273 September/December 2021 OT question
Brett started trading on 1 February 2024. His sales (exclusive of VAT) were £6,000 a month
for the first three months of trading, £8,000 for the next four months and £10,500 a month
after that.
From what date will Brett have to charge output VAT on his supplies?
✅ Answer: D
273 D
Taxable supplies to 30 November 2024 are £81,500 and to 31 December 2024 they are
£92,000. Brett therefore exceeds the registration threshold of £90,000 by the end of
December 2024.
Brett must notify HM Revenue & Customs by 30 January 2025 and he will be registered (and
therefore have to charge VAT) from 1 February 2025.
📋 Examiner’s Report

The other incorrect options are:
A 1 March 2025 is the month after the date from which he must start charging VAT
B 1 January 2025 is the day after the end of the month in which the registration threshold
is breached
C 30 January 2025 is the registration deadline

Q274 · Question 274
+10 XPA · MCQ
274 Betty, a retailer, decides to voluntarily register for VAT.
Which TWO of the following statements, concerning supplies made to Betty before the
date of VAT registration, are TRUE?
still uses for both private and business purposes
business purposes, in the month prior to the date of VAT registration
she still uses in the business
connection with setting up the business
which she sold the week before registration
⚡ Select ALL correct options (B, C)
✅ Answer: B and C
274 B and C
VAT cannot be reclaimed on cars which are used for private purposes.
VAT can normally be reclaimed on fuel used partially for private purposes (although output
VAT will be due based on the fuel scale rate). However, the fuel has been consumed prior to
the date of registration and therefore the input tax cannot be reclaimed.
Input tax can only be reclaimed on goods a nd assets if they are still on hand (or not
consumed) at the date of registration and they were purchased within four years prior to
registration.
Pre-registration input VAT can only be reclaimed on services if they were supplied within six
months of registration.
Pre-registration input VAT can be reclaimed on goods acquired for the business provided they
are on hand (i.e. in inventory) at the date of registration.

Q278 · Question 278
+10 XPA · MCQ
278 Padma Ltd received an order for goods on 20 October 2025. The goods were delivered to the
customer on 20 December 2025 and Padma Ltd sent the invoice for £1,000 on 15 January
2026, which the customer paid on 5 February 2026.
What is the tax point of the transaction for VAT?
✅ Answer: B
278 B
The basic tax point is the date the goods are de livered. This is only overridden by an actual
tax point if a tax invoice is issued or payment is made before the basic tax point or, provided
an actual tax point has not already arisen under the earlier rule, an invoice is issued within
14 days after the basic tax point.

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

A simplified VAT invoice can be provided when the consideration for the supply is less than
£250. A simplified invoice need only show the following information: supplier's name, address
and VAT registration number; the date of supply; a description of the goods or services
supplied; the consideration for the supply; the rate of VAT in force at the time of supply. The
total amount payable needs to be shown on the invoice, but not the amount of VAT.

Q286 · Question 286
+10 XPA · MCQ
286 Following the late submission of the VAT return for the quarter ended 31 October 2025,
Chimney Ltd has three penalty points. For the quarter ended 31 January 2026 the return was
filed on 23 March 2026.
When the 31 January 2026 VAT return is filed late, which of the following consequences
are NOT true?
penalties
£
✅ Answer: B
286 B
Chimney Ltd will have four penalty points after submitting the return for the quarter ended
31 January 2026 late. The company will therefore be charged a £200 penalty and another
penalty will be charged if the following return is submitted late. Penalty points will only be
reset to zero if Chimney Ltd submits all returns on time for the next twelve months.
Penalty points do not expire after two years once the threshold of four penalty points is
reached.

Q291 · Question 291
+10 XPA · MCQ
291 Marina is a UK VAT registered trader making only standard-rated supplies. She purchased
goods worth £10,000 (VAT-exclusive) from a trader situated in Narnia. The goods would be
classed as standard-rated if they were supplied in the UK. The standard rate in Narnia is 5%.
What is the net effect on the VAT position of the UK trader?
✅ Answer: A
291 A
Marina accounts for output VAT of £2,000 as the goods would be standard-rated if supplied
in the UK. She can claim back input VAT of £2,000 on the same return as the goods are used
by a trader that only makes taxable supplies. The net effect on VAT payable is therefore nil.
💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

The rate of VAT in the overseas country is irrelevant. You should always use the rate of VAT
in the UK for calculations.

🔑 Key Answer Tips

This question tests knowledge of a number of VAT issues.
There were some easy marks to be gained in the first two questions for a relatively
straightforward compulsory registration computation and knowledge of the recovery of pre-
registration input VAT.
The next two questions cover the administration of VAT, which again, would provide easy
marks if the rules had been learnt.
The final question focuses on the recovery of input VAT, an area commonly tested.

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

The VAT liability was due on 7 November 2025, but wasn’t paid until 27 November 2025, and
was therefore 20 days late. A penalty is payable on late paid VAT that is more than 15 days
late. The penalty charged is 3% of the late paid VAT for payments between 16 and 30 days
late. This penalty is given in the tax rates and allowances provided in the examination.
Interest is payable from the date the tax should have been paid to the actual date of payment.

VAT can only be recovered on entertaining staff and overseas customers.
Where a leased car has some private use, only 50% of the input VAT can be recovered. The
level of the car’s CO₂ emissions and the percentage of private use are irrelevant.

🔑 Key Answer Tips

This question is really two separate questions and tests knowledge of a number of VAT issues.
There were some easy marks to be gained in the first part for a relatively straightforward
compulsory registration computation and knowledge of the implications of late registration.
The second part of the question is purely computational and tests your knowledge of output
and input VAT, including the rules for pre-registration input VAT.

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

A late registration penalty may be charged. A late submission penalty applies for filing a
return late (which is also consequence of the late registration); but that is separate from the
penalty for late registration.
Output VAT must be accounted for to HM Revenue & Customs from the date that she should
have been registered. Sales from the date of compulsory registration are treated as VAT-
inclusive (even though VAT was not actually charged to customers). Candy can try to recover
the VAT that she should have charged from customers but is not required to do so by HM
Revenue & Customs and indeed it may not be possible.

Where services are used partly for private and partly for business use, an apportionment is
made to calculate the recoverable input VAT.

Pre-registration input VAT can be reclaimed on:
• services supplied within the six months prior to registration, and
• inventory acquired for business purposes in the four years prior to registration that has
not been sold at the time of registration.

The input VAT in respect of the fuel is recoverable in full, despite the private use element.
Output tax will be payable on the fuel scale charge to account for the private use.
The VAT charged on the purchase of the car cannot be recovered but VAT incurred in relation
to repairing the car can be.

All businesses must make their VAT payments electronically and this must be done no later
than one month and seven days after the end of the quarter, i.e. 7 May 2026.

A customer’s VAT registration number is not required to be included on a valid VAT invoice.
The date of delivery of the goods is not automatically required, although this may be the same
date as the tax point, which is required. It is not necessary to include the price inclusive and
exclusive of a prompt payment discount, although some traders choose to include this to
ensure the purchaser accounts for the correct amount of VAT.

The first two questions test the straightforward computation of the VAT payable using the
flat rate scheme percentage, and then the VAT that would have been payable if the normal
basis had been used, and should have provided easy marks to a well-prepared student.
Be careful to read the question carefully thou gh to ascertain whether the figures given are
inclusive or exclusive of VAT.
The third question tests more of the details regarding the flat rate scheme – this sort of
question can only really be answered if the rules have been learnt.
The final two questions test tax points in respect of services and entertaining expenses.

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

Under the flat rate scheme, VAT is calculated by applying a fixed percentage to the turnover
figure inclusive of VAT and including any exempt or zero-rated supplies. Expenses and
purchases are not relevant.



To join the scheme expected taxable turnover ( excluding VAT) for the next 12 months must
not exceed £150,000.
The scheme can be used by both small unincorporated and incorporated businesses.

For services, the basic tax point (BTP) is the date the service is provided/completed.
The actual tax point (ATP) can be either before or after the BTP.
The ATP will be before the BTP if:
• An invoice is issued before the BTP, or
• A payment is received before the BTP (as in this case with the deposit payments).
The ATP will be after the BTP if:
• An invoice is issued with in 14 days of the BTP, or
• The business has an agreement with HMRC for a different date (typically businesses
agree a month end invoicing policy so that the invoice date is usually the ATP).

Input VAT incurred on business entertaining cannot be recovered, with the exceptions of staff
entertaining and entertaining overseas customers.

Are Ltd and Can Ltd can form a group with Knight Ltd for VAT purposes as they are under the
control of Knight Ltd and all of the companies are UK resident. However, eligible companies
are not automatically included in the group. Either Are Ltd or Can Ltd may be excluded.
There will be no need to account for VAT on goods and services supplied between group
members. Such supplies will simply be ignored for VAT purposes.
The group must appoint a representative member who will be responsible for completing one
VAT return for the group. However, the representative could be any of the group companies.
Each group member is jointly and severally liable for the VAT payable by the whole group, not
just its share.

This question covers a variety of VAT topics that are frequently tested, along with the recently
introduced system, making tax digital (MTD). Pre-registration input VAT is a very common
examination topic so make sure that you know the specific rules, as you are unlikely to be
able to correctly guess them!

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

From 1 April 2025 all VAT registered businesses are required to use MTD, whether or not their
turnover exceeds the registration threshold. This means that from that date, any business not
already registered for MTD will now have to keep their VAT records digitally and provide their
VAT return information to HMRC through MTD compatible software.

Input VAT incurred on services in the six months prior to registration can be recovered
provided the services were supplied for business purposes. The input VAT incurred on
advertising costs from 1 April to 30 June is therefore not recoverable.
Input VAT incurred on the acquisition of goods for business purposes can be recovered
provided the goods are acquired no more than four years prior to registration and the goods
are still held at the date of registration. This rule applies equally to capital items as well as
current assets such as inventory and consumables.

The VAT incurred from the point of registration is recoverable regardless of whether the goods
are still in inventory at the end of the VAT quarte r. This is only relevant when determining
whether pre-registration input VAT is recoverable.

All businesses must file their VAT return and pay VAT electronically.
The deadline for filing and payment is one month and seven days after the end of the quarter.

This question requires the calculation of output VAT on sales, input VAT on purchases, and
additional output VAT on goods taken for own use, along with knowledge of simplified VAT
invoice requirements and the flat rate scheme.
When calculating output VAT on sales, make sure you carefully consider the impact of prompt
payment discounts. For input VAT, be aware of the restrictions on recoverability and the rules
regarding services purchased from overseas suppliers.
For goods taken from inventory for personal use, consider which figure output VAT should
be charged on. When dealing with simplifie d VAT invoices, you will need to recall the
essential information that must be included and what can be omitted.

specific flat rate percentage, but it is identify ing the correct figure to apply that percentage
to which is the key point.

Input VAT is reclaimable on marketing services only. The same amount would be accounted

supplied by a company situated overseas, however the question only asks for the input VAT
figure.
No VAT can be reclaimed in respect of the car since it is used partly for private purposes.

Where goods are removed from a business for personal purposes, a taxable supply arises and
the value of that supply of goods for VAT purposes is the replacement value.

A less detailed VAT invoice does not need to show the total amount of VAT charged. The other
items must appear on a simplified invoice.

Under the flat rate scheme, the VAT payable is calculated by applying the flat rate percentage
to the total taxable supplies of the business.

Penalty for late submission
£0 £200

payment
£0 A B
£582 C D
Sub-question 4
If Lian were to use the annual accounting scheme, with a VAT annual return period
ending on 30 June, which VAT advantage could she benefit from?

ended 31 March 2026 in respect of the services purchased from overseas?
✅ Answer: 1: D; 2: B; 3: A; 4: B; 5: D
302 LIAN

1 D
The payment of the deposit on 28 September would have been included in the
quarterly return to 30 September 2025.
The delivery of the equipment on 23 December 2025 is the basic tax point but because
the invoice was raised within 14 days of this, the invoice date becomes the actual tax
point, being 3 January 2026. This will be reported in the quarterly return to 31 March
2026 and not in the return to December 2025.
2 B
Since the claim for the impairment loss is made more than six months after the due
date for payment of 18 June 2025, this output VAT can be reclaimed. The payment due
dates for the other two invoices are not outstanding for more than six months as at
31 December 2025.
3 A
The penalty point in respect of the first late submission for the quarter ended
31 December 2022 will have expired after two years (i.e. by 31 December 2024) as at
that point the threshold of four points had not been reached. The late submissions for
the quarters ended 31 June 2024 and 31 December 2024 each incur a penalty point.
Therefore, the late submission for the quarter ended 31 December 2025 incurs the
third penalty point and there will not yet be a financial penalty.
No penalty for late payment is charged if VAT is paid within 15 days of the due date.
The payment was due on 7 February 2026 and made on 20 February 2026, therefore
no penalty is payable.

4 B
Since only one VAT return is submitted each year under the annual accounting scheme
the reduced administration means that penalties could be avoided in respect of late
submissions. Lian would also have an extra month to submit her return which would
also help with this.

5 D
The services are deemed to be supplied wh ere received, that is the UK. VAT will be
accounted under the reverse charge process with 20% of £4,000 entered as output
VAT and 20% of £4,000 entered as input VAT.
🔑 Key Answer Tips

This is a typical VAT question with lots of calculations, which many learners prefer. It tests
the tax point date, relief for impairment losses, penalties for late submission, annual
accounting and services acquired from overseas.

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

It is the cash accounting scheme which gives automatic relief for impairment losses.
The same amount of VAT is paid under the annual accounting scheme, but over nine monthly
instalments with a balance paid at the same time as the annual return is submitted.
There are instalment payments and a balancing payment under annual accounting.

The overseas rate of VAT will never apply to a supply of services in the UK.

🔑 Key Answer Tips

This VAT question tests the calculation of output VAT when discounts are available and the
recovery of input VAT when there are entertaining and private costs, both of which are
commonly tested areas. The remaining three questions relate to deregistration, the sale of a
business and the impact of a sale as a going concern. These topics are less commonly tested
but would not present too much difficulty to a well-prepared student.

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

60% of customers receive the 10% discount and therefore the calculation of the VAT is based
on 90% of the selling price. VAT is calculated on the exclusive of VAT sales figures and is
therefore at 20%.

Input VAT is allowable on entertaining overseas customers but not for entertaining UK
customers. Input VAT is also not allowable on the private element of the telephone calls.

The new owner can either take over Mabel’s VAT registration, or they may already be
registered. There is no requirement that they must take over Mabel’s registration.
Only if the new owner chooses to take over Mabel’s VAT registration they will also take over
Mabels’s past liabilities (e.g. if she has previously submitted an incorrect return).
Mabel will still have to prepare a VAT return up to the cessation of trade.

🔑 Key Answer Tips

This is a classic ten mark VAT question. A number of easy marks are available for the key facts
and advantages of the VAT cash accounting a nd annual accounting schemes, provided they
are related to the particular circumstances of Silverstone Ltd.
Part (b) covers the overseas aspects of VAT which is relatively straightforward provided the
rules have been learnt.

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

Part (a) – Read the requirement carefully – you are required to explain why the company can
use the schemes and why they will be beneficial. Make sure that you take account of and refer
to the specific circumstances of the company and do not just write about the schemes in
general.
In part (b) use headings in your answer so that it is clear which points relate to each type of
supplier and remember to deal with both when and how to account for VAT for each supplier.
(a) Cash accounting scheme and annual accounting scheme
• Silverstone Ltd can use both schemes because its expected taxable turnover for
the next 12 months does not exceed £1,350,000 exclusive of VAT.
• In addition, for both schemes the company is up to date with its VAT payments
and VAT returns, and for the cash accounting scheme it has not committed any
VAT offences in the last 12 months.
• With the cash accounting scheme, output VAT will be accounted for two months
later than at present since the scheme will result in the tax point becoming the
date that payment is received from customers.
• The recovery of input VAT on expenses will not be affected as these are paid in
cash.
• With the annual accounting scheme, the reduced administration in only having
to file one VAT return each year should save on overtime costs.


(b) 1 Purchase of machinery
• Silverstone Ltd will have to account for output VAT of £4,400 (£22,000 ×
20%) on the VAT return covering the date the goods were imported.
• This will then be reclaimed as input VAT on the same VAT return.

The rate of VAT that would normally apply to sales is irrelevant where they are made to
overseas customers. The supplies will be treated as zero-rated in the UK – the overseas
customer will account for the sales tax in their own country.

You are a trainee Chartered Certified Accountant, and your firm has recently completed its

For the previous three value added tax (VAT) quarters, Tardy plc has been late in submitting
its VAT returns and in paying the related VAT liabilities. The company therefore currently has
three penalty points.
As part of your firm’s tax audit for the year ended 31 March 2026, you have discovered that
Tardy plc has been careless in incorrectly trea ting the supply of standard-rated services
received from VAT registered businesses situated overseas. This careless incorrect treatment
has resulted in an underpayment of VAT to HM Revenue & Customs of £8,200 for the year
ended 31 March 2026.
Required:
(a) Advise Tardy plc of the penalty and interest implications if it is more than 30 days
late in submitting the return and paying the VAT liability for the following quarter,
and state what the company will need to do in order to avoid further penalties.

(4 marks)
(b) Explain when and how a UK VAT registered business should account for VAT
in respect of the supply of services received from overseas VAT registered
businesses.  (3 marks)
(c) Explain why Tardy plc will be permitted to disclose the underpayment of VAT of
£8,200 by entering this amount on its next VAT return.  (1 mark)
(d) Advise Tardy plc as to the maximum amount of penalty which is likely to be charged
by HM Revenue & Customs in respect of the underpayment of VAT of £8,200, and by
how much this penalty would be reduced as a result of the company’s unprompted
disclosure.
 (2 marks)
(Total: 10 marks)
✍️ Constructed response — attempt the full computation in your answer book, then compare with the official solution below.
305 TARDY PLC (ADAPTED) Walk in the footsteps of a top tutor
🔑 Key Answer Tips

This question has four requirements covering various administrative aspects including
penalties and interest, accountin g for supplies of services, disclosure of VAT errors and
penalties for errors. All these aspects should be manageable provided you have learnt the
detailed administration rules. However, make sure you are guided by the marks available,
that you answer the specific question asked and that you base your answer on the facts in
the question, not everything you know about VAT!
In the answers the highlighted words are key phrases that markers are looking for.
(a) Penalties

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

There are multiple separate requirements here – to advise of the penalty implications of a
further late submission; to advise of the penalty and interest implications of a further late
payment and to state what the company needs to do to avoid future penalties. You must
make sure you deal with each requirement and give four clear points to get the four marks
available.
Penalties are tested relatively frequently. The key points to grasp are that there is no penalty
for late submission until the business has four penalty points, but once it has four points,
penalties are payable on each subsequent late submission until the points revert to zero.
The amount of the penalty needs to be learnt as they are not included in the Tax Rates and
Allowances provided in the examination.
And to avoid further penalties, the company will need to submit 4 consecutive returns on time.
In respect of late payment of VAT, both interest and penalties may be payable. The details of
these are provided in your tax tables.
• Tardy plc has already got three penalty points, so a late submission of the next
return will result in four penalty poin ts and therefore a penalty of £200 being
charged.
• VAT being paid more than 30 days late will result in a penalty of 6% of the
overdue VAT, plus a daily penalty at an annual rate of 10%.
• Late payment interest will also be charged at 8.5% for the period until the VAT
is paid.
• In order to avoid future penalties, Tard y plc will need to submit four consecutive
VAT returns on time, the penalty points will then revert to zero.


(b) Supply of services

This part also has two requirements, when and how the VAT should be accounted for. It would
be easy to miss the first part of this requirement, which is actually about tax points, rather
than overseas supplies. Note that the question relates to services, not goods, and therefore
the tax point rules are different.
The second requirement requires an explanation of the reverse charge procedure, by which
VAT is accounted for in the country where the services are carried out.
• VAT should be accounted for on the earliest of the date when the service is
completed, the date the service is paid for, and the date the invoice is issued.
• Output VAT at the UK VAT rate should be declared on the UK business’s VAT
return.
This will then be reclaimed as input VAT on the same VAT return, so the effect
will be VAT neutral.
This is known as the reverse charge procedure.
(c) Errors on a VAT return

The requirement here is to explain why the error can be disclosed on the next return, which
means applying the de minimis test to the amount of the error. Since the error is less than
£10,000, the company’s turnover figure is not required.
• Tardy plc will be permitted to disclose the underpayment of VAT of £8,200 by
entering this amount on its next VAT return as the net error is less than the limit
of £10,000.


(d) VAT penalties

This question covers the standard penalty for an incorrect return. The same penalty system
applies to income tax, NICs, corporation tax and VAT and could be tested in relation to any of
those taxes. Note that the penalties for errors are included in the Tax Rates and Allowances
provided in the examination.
Here you are asked for the maximum amount of the penalty, which depends upon the
taxpayer’s behaviour and also by how much it could be reduced by an unprompted disclosure.
Again, make sure you cover both points in your answer.
• Tardy plc has been careless in its incorrect treatment of the supply of services
received, so the maximum amount of penalty will therefore be 30% of the VAT
underpaid (£8,200 × 30% = £2,460).
• However, this penalty could be reduced to £0 as a result of the company’s
unprompted disclosure to HM Revenue & Customs.

trading company, to his son, Gran t. The market value of the shares on that date was £240,000.
Delroy had subscribed for the 25,000 shares in Dub Ltd at par on 1 July 2015. Delroy and Grant have
elected to hold over the gain as a gift of a business asset.
Grant sold the 25,000 shares in Dub Ltd on 18 March 2026 for £240,000.
Dub Ltd has a share capital of 100,000 £1 ordinary shares. Delroy was the sales director of the
company from its incorporation on 1 July 2015 until 10 January 2026. Grant has never been an
employee or a director of Dub Ltd.
For the tax year 2025/26, Delroy and Grant are both higher rate taxpayers. They have each made
other disposals of assets during the tax year 2025/26, and therefore they have both already utilised
their annual exempt amount for this year.
Marlon and Alvita
On 28 March 2026, Marlon sold a house for £497,000, which he had owned individually. The house
had been purchased on 22 October 2010 for £152,600.
Throughout the period of ownership, the house was occupied by Marlon and his wife, Alvita, as
their main residence. One-third of the house was always used exclusively for business purposes by
the couple. Business asset disposal relief is not available in respect of this disposal.
For the tax year 2025/26, Marlon is a higher rate taxpayer, but Alvita did not have any taxable
income. This will remain the case for the tax year 2026/27. Neither of them has made any other
disposals of assets during the year.

🔑 Key Answer Tips

A classic VAT question covering the preparation of a VAT return and the flat rate scheme.
Part (a) requires the calculation of VAT payable by a sole trader for a year.
Part (b) considers why the flat rate scheme may be an option and requires knowledge of the
conditions.
Part (c) requires a calculation to prove whether or not it would be advantageous to join the
scheme.
The highlighted words in parts (b) and (c) are key phrases that markers are looking for.

💡 Tutor’s Top Tips

In this type of question, read the question carefully and find out whether the figures given are
inclusive of VAT (as in this question) or exclusive of VAT.

– Zero-rated 0

Make sure you memorise the conditions and thresholds for the various VAT schemes which
provide easy marks as long as you have learnt them.
This requirement has two parts (joining and leaving the flat rate scheme), so be sure that you
address both parts.
• Zia can join the flat rate scheme from 1 April 2026 because his taxable turnover
(excluding VAT) for the next 12 months is not expected to exceed £150,000.
• He can continue to use the scheme until his total turnover (including VAT, but
excluding sales of capital assets) for the previous year exceeds £230,000.

It is also necessary to leave the flat scheme if total turnover is expected to exceed £230,000
during the following 30 days.
Although candidates are not expected to be aware of this point, equivalent marks were
awarded if this was given instead of the previous year limit.


(c) Flat rate scheme – benefits

The notes underneath the requirement give a strong hint to recalculate the liability using the
flat rate given. Remember to then conclude whether or not it would have been beneficial to
have used the scheme.
• Using the flat rate scheme to calculate his VAT liability, Zia would have paid VAT
of £15,120 (£126,000 × 12%) for the year ended 31 March 2026.
• It would therefore not have been beneficial to use the flat rate scheme as the
additional cost of £6,260 (£15,120 – £8,860) for the year would appear to
outweigh the advantage of simplified VAT administration.

Under the flat rate scheme Zia would be required to pay the flat rate percentage of his VAT-
inclusive turnover (including zero-rated supplies) with no deductions for input VAT.

Important:

Where companies do not have coterminous (matching) year ends, the available profits and
losses must be time apportioned, to find the relevant amounts falling within the
corresponding accounting period.

The profit threshold is shared between associated companies, in this case two. Sizeable Ltd
exceeded the threshold of £750,000 (£1,500,000/2) in the current and the previous period.
As this is not the first period that Sizeable Ltd is a large company, the corporation tax must
be settled by paying quarterly instalments. The instalments are based on the estimated
corporation tax liability for the current accounting period.

As Lateness Ltd is not a large company, the corporation tax would have been due 9 months
and 1 day after the end of the accounting period (1 October 2026).

The chattels rules apply to the disposal of the antique table. The gross proceeds are ˃£6,000
and the cost is ≤£6,000 therefore the treatment is as follows:
The gain is calculated as normal i.e. Proceeds – cost
The gain must not exceed the maximum amount of 5/3 × (gross proceeds – £6,000)

Opal’s estate is reduced by the available nil rate band of £105,000 (£325,000 – £220,000).
The PET on 7 November 2025 reduces the nil rate band available as it is within seven years of
the date of death. The previous PET is more than seven years before death.
Opal also qualifies for the full residence nil rate band as she is leaving her main residence to
her direct descendants and it is valued in excess of £175,000.

If Opal were to live until 20 March 2033 the PET on 7 November 2025 would no longer be
chargeable and would result in an additional available nil rate band on death of £220,000.
25 2 and 3

The basic tax point for a supply of services is the date when they are completed, but if a VAT
invoice is issued or payment received before the basic tax point, then this becomes the actual
tax point. Therefore, the tax point for the additional contract is when the VAT invoice was
issued on 1 March.

Glacier Ltd was late in submitting VAT returns for three previous quarters and therefore
already has three penalty points. None of these points are more than two years old and
therefore none have expired. When submitting the return for the quarter ended 31 March
2026 late, Glacier Ltd reaches the threshold of four penalty points and will be charged a £200
penalty.

Glacier Ltd must issue a VAT invoice when it makes a standard-rated supply to a VAT
registered customer. However, there is no requirement to do so if the supply is exempt or if
the supply is to a non-VAT registered customer.
A VAT invoice should be issued within 30 days of the date when the supply is treated as being
made.
